#1305. ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Maresca said: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”

When asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca said: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

#1304. Harry Kane Names the Major Trophy He'd Happily 'Trade' His Ballon d'Or For

It's been a fantastic few seasons for Harry Kane, culminating in his 2026 Ballon d'Or win.

The English striker scored goal after goal for Tottenham Hotspur, but never managed to get his hands on a major trophy with Spurs. In the pursuit of glory, he made the move to Bayern Munich in 2023, and that has proved to be a sensible transfer.

The 33-year-old, one of the oldest Ballon d'Or winners, has now won two Bundesliga titles and the DFB-Pokal, while continuing to score at an electrifying rate. Indeed, Kane scored 73 goals for club and country in 2025/26, which helped him win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Lamine Yamal may have won, but some former Ballon d'Or winners didn't even include him in their top three.

Having been named the world's best player, the Englishman could not hide his delight, saying he was 'speechless' as he claimed the award in London. However, in the short time since that historic night, Kane has revealed that he would swap the Ballon d'Or for one major honour.

Speaking to reporters via Goal, he claimed that he'd happily 'trade' his prize if it meant winning the Champions League with Bayern. Kane explained:

"Team trophies are why we play football. The team aspect of our sport is really, really important. The Ballon d'Or last week was one of the best feelings I've had in my life and my career... but to have moments with the team, celebrations with the club, to be able to lift the Champions League with Bayern would be an incredible feeling.

"Of course the Ballon d'Or is a highlight, it puts me on an even bigger level, but you want to have these big finals, the Champions League, having that feeling of emotion with your teammates as well. I would choose the Champions League, but I have the opportunity to do both, let's see what happens."

That's not to say Kane isn't appreciating the value of his award, as he went on to add: "Winning the Ballon d'Or was a huge achievement for me. I've had to overcome many challenges in my career, some people didn't think I'd get this far..."

Kane most notably made it all the way to the Champions League final with Spurs in 2018/19, but was unable to get across the line, as his team lost 2-0 to Liverpool. At the time, he dejectedly said:

“It was a tough one to take. It’s probably one of the biggest games we’ll ever play in our careers and to let it slide by is always a tough one to take. It’s an experience we need to learn from."

At Bayern, Kane then made it to the semis twice, and the quarters once, but still hasn't been able to make another final. He's also suffered more disappointment in cup competitions with England.

Once again, his goalscoring record at that level has never been questioned – he is the Three Lions' all-time top scorer after all – but he's lost two finals with his country, suffering defeat at both Euro 2020 and Euro 2024. He also made it to the semis with England this summer at the 2026 World Cup, but once again fell short when it came to pushing for glory.

With all that disappointment in mind, it's little wonder Kane would happily give up his Ballon d'Or if it meant finally getting his hands on a major team honour such as the Champions League.

#1303. Chivu: ‘Inter are still in the Champions League race, we’ll have a great game against Feyenoord’

Cristian Chivu insists Inter are “still in the race” in the Champions League, and has backed his players to respond to Saturday’s derby defeat in Rotterdam on Tuesday.

With quotes courtesy of the Corriere dello Sport, the Inter coach spoke at his pre-match press conference before the game against Feyenoord at De Kuip. It kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Inter are under pressure on two fronts. Saturday’s 3-1 loss to Milan was their first league defeat of the season. In Europe they have only three points from three games, after a late win over Shakhtar Donetsk and defeats to Real Madrid and Club Brugge.

“I believe in the work, in what this team is and what it has done so far. I’m confident. They’re champions, and they’ve shown it,” Chivu said. “There have been negative episodes and mistakes that we have to learn from, accept and move past, trying to fix them. But I’m confident.”

Chivu believes 16 points will be enough for a top-eight finish and a place in the round of 16.

“We’ve always said that the Champions League, like the league, has to be played game by game. To get into the top eight, it’s around 16 points,” he said. “For now we’ve won one game and lost two, but we’re still in it. We know what we are and what we want, and I’m convinced we’ll have a great game.”

He warned that Giovanni van Bronckhorst’s Feyenoord, who beat Como at home earlier in the competition, will be dangerous. “In this stadium they thrive. They have intensity, quality and a lot of players like Moussa and Zequiel. They’re quality players and inverted wingers. It won’t be easy, but at the same time we have to bring out all our qualities to put them in difficulty.”

“We’ve had to deal with some unpredictable situations and look for solutions with what we had available. We’ve got Provedel and Pavard back, and fortunately we haven’t had any problems in the last few days.”

#1302. Exclusive: Nick Montgomery On Managing In China And Working Under Postecoglou

Beijing Guoan are unbeaten in 21 games in all competitions, and last month's trip to Henan showed exactly why. Three goals down at half-time, Nick Montgomery’s side scored four times after the break. Zhang Yuning got the 81st-minute winner. It was the first time in Guoan's 33-year history they had ever won from three goals down.

It caps a superb first season in China for 44-year-old head coach Nick Montgomery. He won the Chinese FA Super Cup – China’s version of the Community Shield – in his first competitive game in March, and Guoan are also unbeaten through three games in the AFC Champions League Elite tournament. Thai side Port FC are up next on Tuesday.

Only a five-point deduction for historical breaches, handed down after Montgomery arrived, has kept Guoan out of the title race. Without it, they would go into the final-day fixture on November 8 against Chongqing Tonglianglong top of the table, ahead of current leaders Chengdu Rongcheng on goal difference. Instead, they are third, two points behind Dalian Yingbo, with a Chinese FA Cup semi-final against Shanghai Port to come on November 20.

A former Sheffield United midfielder, Montgomery won the A-League as a head coach with Central Coast Mariners and the Europa League as Postecoglou’s assistant at Tottenham. Now he is making his name in China.

Montgomery did not need much convincing. He had played in Beijing with the Mariners, and the memory never left him.

“If we’re talking about Beijing Guoan, we’re talking about one of the biggest clubs in Asian football, and it’s a club I know well because of my time playing in the A-League,” he told GIVEMESPORT. “I played in the Asian Champions League, and I remember, I think it was a Wednesday night, playing in Beijing. There were 40,000 fans, and that always stuck in my mind.”

After leaving Nottingham Forest, where he was Ange Postecoglou's assistant, Montgomery had plenty of offers but was waiting for the right one. It came from Matthias Brosamer, the German who had just been appointed Guoan’s new sporting director.

"He is a great guy, very intelligent. He speaks fluent Chinese, and we had some amazing football conversations," said Montgomery, who was appointed on 8 January. “He told me about the project. He was looking for a head coach with experience in Asia, and he really loved my profile. Things moved forward quickly, and probably within a week or two we’d agreed to take on the project. I was landing in Beijing in wintertime – I think it was minus 20 when I arrived – and that was the start of such an exciting journey.”

Working largely through translators, Montgomery knew his first job was to win people over. It didn't take him long.

“When you come into a new country, you’ve got to be brave to start with,” he said. “You’ve got to know there’s a period where you’ll have to get everybody to buy in – to you as a person, forget the football – because you’re coming into their culture. If they see you’re committed and believe in your style of football, then they’re going to support you. I have created a real family environment, which is important.”

The start could hardly have gone better. Guoan’s Super Cup triumph came against Shanghai Port, winners of the last three Chinese Super League titles, who were beaten 2-0 in Nanjing.

“We beat Shanghai Port, who were the benchmark team. They had players picking up ridiculous salaries over the years, the best squads,” said Montgomery, who knows Port boss Kevin Muscat from their days in Australia. “That was the first real game, so to win a trophy was a great start.”

Injuries soon took their toll, though, and Guoan won just four of their first 14 league games, the last of those a 2-1 home defeat by Henan on 23 May. They have not lost since.

“People said you can’t play like this in China, that the players are not resilient enough, and I never believed that,” he said. “The players showed me on the training ground every day. We don’t speak about being 21 games unbeaten. We just focus on the process.”

The biggest change has come up front, where Montgomery has paired China captain Zhang Yuning with Angola international Fábio Abreu.

“I always played in Australia with two strikers, and I play in China with two strikers, which I was told no one did before,” he said. “I was told they couldn’t play together. The previous season, only one of them played and the other was on the bench. Now they’re both top scorers in the team.”

Unfortunately, Guoan lost Abreu in mid-October after he broke his leg in a 1-0 win against Qingdao West Coast.

"We were very sad," said Montgomery. "He will miss the rest of the season. Most of our injuries have been contact ones, which is very unlucky. We have had to deal with many challenges this season, and that makes our form even more satisfying."

Guoan's numbers speak for themselves. They are also at or near the top of the league for possession, forward passes and touches in the opposition box.

“If the players don’t want to run for you, you’re never going to have those statistics,” Montgomery said. “That tells you Chinese players are honest. If they believe in you, they’ll do everything you ask.”

It is all the more impressive given Guoan started on minus five points – a deduction neither Montgomery nor Brosamer knew about when they took over.

“It was a bit of a shock to everybody. You’re on minus points before you even get to zero,” he said. “If we’d started on a level playing field, we’d be top of the league."

The title may be out of reach, but Montgomery will feel encouraged that, without the deduction, Beijing Guoan would be top. Second place is still possible if Guoan win their last league game againstChongqing Tonglianglong and Dalian Yingbo lose or draw. And there is the chance to defend the Chinese FA Cup, which Gooan won for the sixth time last season when they beat Henan 3-0 under former coach Quique Setien.

“We can’t win the league because of what happened, which is a shame, but we can still finish second,” Montgomery said. “In the cup, we’ve got a difficult game against Shanghai Port. They were the Galácticos of the Chinese Super League for the last couple of years. Players like Oscar and Hulk – all the big names – loved playing in China.”

In the AFC Champions League, Guoan beat Pohang Steelers 3-1 in the first Asian Champions League game at the Workers’ Stadium for seven years, before winning 1-0 at Buriram United – “a very difficult place to go”, according to Montgomery. They drew 2-2 with Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors on October 27 and are currently fifth in the league phase.

Montgomery is clearly relishing life in China, where Guoan have drawn crowds of more than 60,000 at the rebuilt Workers’ Stadium this season.

“What the Western world thinks of China is the total opposite of the reality. It’s so advanced,” he said. “The infrastructure in football is unbelievable. Our home games get 50,000 to 65,000 on a weekly basis. There aren’t many Premier League teams that can match that attendance. It is one of the best stadiums in the world – very similar to the Tottenham stadium, which I know very well.

“And there is the belief, moving forward, that the club can bring a championship back to Beijing for the first time since 2009, which is a long time ago.”

Montgomery made the decision that he wanted to return to work as a No.1 again after spending time as Ange Postecoglou's assistant at both Tottenham Hotspur (2024-2025) and Nottingham Forest (2025).

“It’s not like I would be an assistant for any manager,” he said. “I did get asked about being an assistant to another manager, but it wasn’t for me. I knew I was waiting for the right opportunity to get back into management.”

His route to Tottenham began with a message from Postecoglou, who was among the first to congratulate him when the Mariners won the A-League in 2023. A year later, Postecoglou’s assistant Chris Davies left to become Birmingham City manager.

“As with anything in life, it’s about timing,” Montgomery said. “Ange contacted me, we jumped on a call, and he said, ‘I’m going to win a trophy at Tottenham. I want you to come and help me.’ To be honest, I didn’t really need to think about it much. It was a pretty quick decision, and one I definitely don’t regret. Seeing the Tottenham fans at the parade with the trophy was something you can never forget.”

That parade followed Brennan Johnson’s winner against Manchester United in the Europa League final in Bilbao in May 2025, which ended Spurs’ 17-year wait for a trophy – even as an injury-ravaged side finished 17th in the Premier League.

“There was an unbelievable amount of injuries, and the squad was very, very thin,” said Montgomery, who joined in June 2024 with his long-time assistant Sergio Raimundo. “We had some big results, beating Man City 4-0 away and Man United 3-0, but after the injuries came, it was difficult. Winning the Europa League would get the club Champions League football, so you put all your eggs in one basket. As a staff, that’s what we all did. We believed we could win it, and that’s what we did.

“I think only now, or years after, will people look back and think what an amazing achievement that was, because it’s been a difficult ride since then – when you look at the amount of money they’ve spent.”

Even that was not enough to save Postecoglou, who was sacked 16 days after the final. Montgomery admits the staff saw it coming.

“Ange came out and said it in an interview, so for sure – everyone knew there was going to be a change no matter what happened,” he said. “So you have that laser focus on what you can control, and that was winning the Europa League. It was amazing for the club to get Champions League football the following season – it’s just a shame they didn’t give Ange and us that chance. But that’s football. You move on.”

When Postecoglou took over at Nottingham Forest in September 2025, Montgomery went with him, alongside Raimundo and fellow Spurs assistant Mile Jedinak. The Australian was sacked after 39 days and eight games without a win.

Asked what went wrong, Montgomery chose his words carefully.

“Probably the least I say, the better on that one,” he said. “It’s a club with a passionate owner [Evangelos Marinakis] that wants instant success, and it’s a club that is renowned for making changes – a lot of changes, as we’ve seen. So you’re never going to go in thinking, ‘This is a stable environment.’

“I was literally about to take an offer of a head coach role, and Ange said: ‘I think it’s a young squad, we can play good football, and I’d love you to come in with me again.’ It was a big boost, because we’d just come off the back of winning the Europa League. We all went in there wanting to do something, but there wasn’t much time.”

Forest have since been through Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira, with Oliver Glasner appointed in July as their fifth head coach in less than a year.

“A lot of the performances were very good, but the results didn’t match them,” Montgomery added. “These type of projects depend on how much time people are willing to give you, and in the end, you’re not in control of that.”

One player he loved briefly working with was Elliot Anderson, who joined Manchester City for a reported £116m this summer.

“Elliot is a magnificent player, and I still keep in touch with him now. He literally never stops running and is brave on the ball – he just wants it all the time,” said Montgomery. “I think he’s definitely one of the best English midfielders I’ve seen, because he can do everything.”

Before Tottenham came Hibernian. Montgomery left Central Coast for Easter Road in September 2023, taking over a side who had lost their opening three league games.

“I had a lot of offers to go to Japan and other places, but I’ve got Scottish heritage in my family, and Hibs is a big club that hasn't had much success in a long time,” he said. “I was promised a rebuild. The club was bottom of the league and in a bit of a mess. I started well and took the team into the top three at one point. Then there was the Africa Cup of Nations and the Asian Cup, and we lost half the starting players.

“I felt I was building something really good, but we just missed out on the top six with the last kick of the ball. Then I had differences of opinion with the club over what had been promised in terms of the rebuild. You have the owner who wants his way, and in the end we chose to part ways. I moved on, went to Tottenham and won the Europa League. Everything happens for a reason.”

That last kick was Shane Blaney’s stoppage-time equaliser for Motherwell in April 2024, which let Dundee pip Hibs to the final top-six place. Hibs finished eighth, and Montgomery departed the following month – but he holds no grudges.

“I always believe every experience is a good experience – good, bad or indifferent,” he said. “Trust is a big thing for me. If you lose that trust, it’s difficult. But you grow from every experience.”

Montgomery’s methods were forged down under. After 12 years at Sheffield United, he joined Central Coast Mariners in 2012 and helped them win their first A-League Championship a year later. He made 133 appearances in all competitions and captained the club, then coached its academy side before stepping up to the top job in 2021. Two years later, he delivered the Mariners’ first title since his playing days.

“There were big teams spending a lot of money, like Sydney FC, Melbourne Victory and Melbourne City, and we were, comparatively, a small club,” he said. “As a coach, the club had suffered a lot of bottom-of-the-table finishes, with no budget compared to the other teams. I always believed I would take over the youth team, develop the players and push them into the first team when I got the opportunity for the job, and that came within two years.

“In my second season, we brought a lot more young players through and recruited some good foreign players. Jason Cummings, who many people will know in Scotland, was our top scorer. We beat Melbourne City 6-1 in the final with the youngest squad and lowest budget in history to win the championship, which was a massive achievement, and it made me really believe in myself as a coach.”

Cummings, the former Hibs striker, scored a hat-trick in that 2023 Grand Final, delivering the Mariners’ first title since Montgomery’s playing days a decade earlier.

“I never look too far ahead. One thing I remember Ange saying is: ‘They’ll only ever remember the people who win silverware.’ I think that’s true,” he said. “If you don’t win silverware, nobody really remembers your stint there. So making history with the three trophies I’ve been involved in, in such a short period of time as a young manager, makes you cherish those moments, because a lot of players and coaches go through their whole career without ever winning a trophy."

The excellent job Montgomery is currently doing is sure to catch the eye of other clubs around the world, including back in England. He is settled, and solely focused on some big games ahead to close this season with Guoan. Yet in the long run, the chance to manage in the Premier League would be hard to turn down.

“For me, I just take each day as it comes," he said. "For sure, maybe one day I would love to manage in the Premier League. But for now, being China is huge for me. I can't think of a better job right now for me, to be honest. I have a great sporting director [Brosamer] and president, Zhou Jinhui. They both support me and really believe in what I am doing.”

Once the domestic campaign ends, the AFC Champions League continues and will run on into next season. Should Guoan go deep, the finals are due to be held in Saudi Arabia next spring – where Postecoglou’s Al Nassr could be waiting.

“For me to represent Beijing, the capital of China, and get through to the knockout stage would be a huge moment for Chinese football,” he said. “There’s a long way to go, but who knows? It would definitely be good to see Ange if that happened.”

Almost two years on from Bilbao, it would be quite the reunion.

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER and ISAAN KHAN, REPORTER

Published: 13:51 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 04:02 EDT, 2 November 2026

Arsenal's miserly defence thwarted Liverpool at Anfield to send the Premier League champions three points clear at the top.

Kai Havertz tapped in the winner from a fine Arsenal move 16 minutes in, with Alexis Mac Allister spurning Liverpool's best chance to equalise before the break.

Wave after wave of attack from the home side came and went in the second period, although Andoni Iraola's men were unable to conjure many clear-cut chances, and they failed to have a single shot on target.

The Gunners took advantage of Man City's defeat by Brighton on Saturday and now have clear water between themselves and the chasing pack.

So who shone the most on an attritional and potentially pivotal afternoon in the title race?

Daily Mail Sport's LEWIS STEELE and ISAAN KHAN were in position at Anfield to run the rule over both sides...

Ezri Konsa (left) and Gabriel Magalhaes (right) were at the heart of Arsenal's resilient win

A loose pass cost Liverpool and led directly to Arsenal’s goal but he made a phenomenal save on 73 minutes to deny Christos Tzolis.

A few heavy touches early doors but the youngster settled in and made some important tackles.

Made a last-ditch intervention on 71 minutes to prevent what looked certain to be Arsenal's second goal.

Threatened more than usual going forward and nearly had an assist, but a bad Alexis Mac Allister header flew over when he should have done far better.

Two fouls were lucky to go unpunished in the opening stages but Nyoni, on his first league start, soon settled and started to dictate from deep.

Trey Nyoni made a shaky start for the Reds but quickly found his composure

Had Liverpool’s best chance when unmarked in the box and the Argentine usually gobbles up those chances. Was Liverpool’s sharpest player.

Did an important defensive shift up against wildcard left-back Riccardo Calafiori, who is everywhere, but Gakpo did not offer enough threat the other way.

Another big game where fans would have wanted more. Some nice moments but he made the wrong decision too often.

Had a big opening just after Arsenal’s goal to make it 1-1 but a heavy touch let him down. Was Liverpool’s most dangerous asset in the first half, then looked tired late on.

Bradley Barcola was the most dangerous Liverpool attacker but fatigue set in

His honesty came back to bite him when he did not throw himself to ground in a first-half penalty shout. Did not impact proceedings enough otherwise.

Dominik Szoboszlai (for Nyoni, 58min) - 6

His attackers got into dangerous positions but could not finish their dinner.

Accurate, fast distribution when under pressure from the Liverpool frontline. Consistently set Arsenal away on counter-attacks.

Looked overwhelmed at times and didn’t get forward as much as he’d have liked. Still, played his part in keeping the cleansheet.

Bailed out by Declan Rice for his errant pass on 18 minutes. After that, he barely put a foot wrong. Found himself in the right place at the right time defensively.

Up for the fight in the bearpit atmosphere that is Anfield. Strong aerially and stayed switched on for darting runs of Isak.

A handful both in attack and defence. Made menacing runs into final third which the opposition found tricky to track.

A complete, domineering display typified by a desire to break into attacking areas and clean up in midfield. Excellent cross to assist Havertz.

Declan Rice celebrates the first Arsenal win at Anfield in 14 years after full time

Good effort by the Greek to accelerate his return to Arsenal’s squad after his injury woes. Curling effort on 73 minutes required a fantastic save.

Christos Tzolis looked on in disbelief after Alisson saved brilliantly from his effort

Simple finish from Rice’s excellent cross. Did his best to hold play up when in possession. Put in a vigorous shift off the ball.

Arsenal win at Anfield for the first time in 14 years, and they kept a clean sheet. An excellent day’s work.

#1300. Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits2, prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions3,4,5. Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

Emotion regulation is a core determinant of mental and physical health1. It encompasses the strategies that people use, intentionally or automatically, to influence their emotional experience. Among these, cognitive reappraisal—changing the interpretation of a situation to alter its emotional impact—has received particular attention in psychology, psychiatry and the broader public. It is central to cognitive-behavioural therapy and linked to resilience, lower symptom burden and improved daily affect1.

Neuroimaging studies have extensively mapped the neural basis of reappraisal. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) consistently implicates a network of lateral and medial prefrontal regions, often along with reduced amygdala activation during reappraisal of negative stimuli2. These findings have informed neuromodulatory interventions for emotion regulation deficits6,7,8. Still, they are based primarily on within-person designs that contrast experimental conditions such as ‘reappraise’ versus ‘view without regulation’ in the same individuals, and many studies and broader theories extend these neural within-person mechanisms to explain between-person individual differences in well-being or psychopathology4,5. This extension is not necessarily warranted.

Extending within-person neural mechanisms to explain between-person differences risks the ecological fallacy9: associations at one level need not hold at the other. For instance, people who habitually use reappraisal report better well-being than others. However, in daily life, reappraisal often occurs in response to stressors and may therefore coincide with worse-than-average momentary mood.

Compounding this, prefrontal regions that are engaged during reappraisal also participate in working memory, response selection and pain processing10—limiting their specificity as emotion-related markers of regulatory function. Task designs, moreover, may not mirror naturalistic regulation, raising questions about ecological validity and relevance for individual-difference research11,12. A recent systematic review found partial effect convergence in prefrontal and amygdala circuits, but studies were underpowered13 (median n = 25) and too heterogeneous for formal meta-analysis3. In turn, meta-analyses on reappraisal in mental disorders have yielded mixed results, with inconsistent findings in the prefrontal cortex4,14,15.

To resolve this, we conducted a preregistered consortium analysis of 40 fMRI datasets on the neurobiology of emotion regulation capacity (NIDER consortium; n = 2,175;  Methods, ‘Consortium procedures’ and Supplementary Table 1)—approximately 20 times larger than previous efforts3—with sufficient power to detect even small between-person associations (r = 0.10; Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’). In this context, reappraisal capacity refers to individual differences in whether, and how effectively, people use reappraisal to reduce negative affect. We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal. Prior work has linked these three indices with each other and with prefrontal activity during reappraisal3,16,17,18,19. To our knowledge, this assumption has not been tested at scale. Notably, the most widely used trait questionnaires are generally understood to index self-reported habitual tendencies to reappraise rather than the ability to implement reappraisal. We nonetheless included them given their proposed functional link to such ability16,17,18 and their widespread use.

We explored whether the three indices converge on a shared core, and whether any of them relate to activity in canonical emotion regulation circuits during common reappraisal tasks2. Our findings have direct implications for neuromodulatory interventions, biomarker development and the validity of individual-difference research in affective neuroscience.

In a first step, we aimed to assess the overlap between the three main indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation. If these three indices represent a similar core construct, or are otherwise functionally related, they should show a meaningful association. Individual consortium study teams calculated the correlations between the three indices of reappraisal capacity based on a standardized coding protocol using functionally predefined regions of interest, ensuring that higher values on each index indicate higher reappraisal capacity. Study-level results were aggregated with random-effects meta-analyses, which is statistically equivalent to person-level random-effects mega-analysis for the preregistered analyses and was intended to circumvent data sharing thresholds (Supplementary Methods, ‘Meta- vs mega-analytic approaches’). The evidence for null results was further quantified using Bayes factors (Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’).

There was a statistically significant association between amygdala down-regulation and task-based affective ratings (P = 0.010; Table 1 and Forest plots in Extended Data Figs. 1–3). As hypothesized, participants with stronger down-regulation of the amygdala via cognitive reappraisal showed a better down-regulation of task-based affective ratings. Yet, the effect size was comparatively small (r = 0.08): To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80%, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

There was no significant association between trait questionnaires and either outcome—that is, amygdala down-regulation or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.06, BF10 ≤ 0.16; Table 1). Confidence intervals ruled out even small effect sizes (r = 0.10), for which statistical power was above 88% given the maximal observed between-study heterogeneity (τ = 0.07; Supplementary Fig. 1). The overlap (shared variance) between the three indices of cognitive reappraisal capacity is shown in Fig. 1, which indicates no shared overlap between all three. Bayes factors substantially favoured the null hypothesis for associations with trait questionnaires (BF10 ≤ 0.16). Between-study heterogeneity was not statistically significant in any of the three tests (P > 0.17) and was particularly small for the non-significant correlations (τ = 0.00 and 0.06), indicating that these null findings are unlikely to be explained by differences in study design.

Pairwise overlap between three widely used indices of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation. Overlap is shown as shared variance derived from the corresponding pairwise random-effects meta-analytic Pearson correlations, which are displayed next to each intersection. The correlations were: task-based affective ratings with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.08, P = 0.010, k = 26, n = 1,377; trait questionnaires with task-based affective ratings, r = 0.05, P = 0.067, k = 28, n = 1,397; and trait questionnaires with amygdala down-regulation, r = 0.01, P = 0.807, k = 33, n = 1,833. All tests were two-sided and uncorrected.

All studies made use of trait questionnaires that primarily assess beliefs about habitual reappraisal use. Although relations to implementation ability, as measured by experiments, are theoretically and empirically expected16,17,18, trait questionnaires that directly measure beliefs about such abilities might show stronger associations. To test this, we performed a subsequent analysis based on three large studies that additionally administered modified versions of the emotion regulation questionnaire to capture such beliefs about abilities20. Fixed-effects meta-analysis confirmed that beliefs about habitual use and implementation ability are strongly related (r = 0.67; Table 1). Supporting the null results for habit questionnaires, there was substantial evidence against an association between these ability trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings (BF10 = 0.13). By contrast, the association between trait ability questionnaires and amygdala down-regulation was statistically significant (P = 0.010), but in the opposite direction, meaning that beliefs in higher reappraisal capacity were related to less effective down-regulation of the amygdala. This represents strong evidence against an effect in the expected direction (one-sided BF10 = 0.05).

To address the second research question, we examined whether individual differences in the three reappraisal indices were systematically related to neural activity during cognitive reappraisal beyond the amygdala. We first tested these associations in canonical emotion regulation networks derived from prior meta-analytic work2 (Fig. 2a) and then complemented these confirmatory analyses with exploratory whole-brain analyses, both outlined in the preregistration (Methods, ‘Statistical analyses’). This strategy was intended to assess whether the three indices showed associations with established regulatory circuitries and whether any observed effects converged on overlapping or distinct neural regions.

a, A priori emotion regulation networks derived from a previous meta-analysis2 and used as the predefined networks of interest. b–d, Brain-wide Pearson correlations between activation during reappraisal relative to negative viewing (reappraise negative − view negative) and three commonly used indices of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires (b; k = 37, n = 2,091), task-based affective ratings (c; k = 31, n = 1,958) and amygdala down-regulation (d; k = 35, n = 2,088). Significant associations are shown at the whole-brain level after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q < 0.05, two-sided). All significant effects were negative. The shared colour bar indicates Pearson’s r, with more intense colours reflecting stronger negative correlations. The colour bar was truncated at −0.30 for visibility reasons, although larger negative correlations were frequent for amygdala down-regulation (d). For the full distribution of correlations with amygdala down-regulation, see Extended Data Fig. 5. In d, negative correlations reflect positive associations with amygdala responses during reappraisal as amygdala down-regulation was coded using the inverse contrast [view negative − reappraise negative]. Slices are displayed in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space: x = 4, y = 0, z = 0 (a); x = 4, y = 0, z = 0 (b); x = −44, y = 7, z = 4 (c); x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 (d). Anatomical backgrounds are based on the MNI152 template (© 1993–2009 Louis Collins, McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, Montreal Neurological Institute, McGill University).

There was no statistically significant association between trait questionnaires and neural activity during reappraisal (Fig. 2b). The correlations with average activity in the two predefined networks were negligibly small and the null hypothesis strongly favoured by Bayes factors (both |r| ≤ 0.03, P > 0.25, uncorrected, BF10 < 0.02; k = 37, n = 2,091). No voxels survived the correction for multiple comparisons in the voxel-wise networks of interest or the whole-brain approach. All brain-wide effect sizes were smaller than |r| = 0.11 (mean = −0.01, range −0.10 to 0.09).

These null results were stable when using a jackknife procedure—that is, no statistically significant voxels when repeating the meta-analysis while leaving out one study at a time. They were further supported by Bayesian posterior odds for voxels across the canonical emotion regulation networks2 (that is, Bayes factors corrected for multiple comparisons; Methods, ‘Bayesian evidence’). The null hypothesis was decisively favoured for 98% of voxels with odds over 100:1, there were no voxels with favourable odds for the existence of an effect, and only two voxels favoured the null in an ambiguous range below 3:1. The power to detect a small effect (r = 0.10) was 96% for average network responses (τ = 0.07). Power in voxel-wise analyses was mostly above 80% in simulated scenarios for this effect size, especially for the network of interest approach (Supplementary Methods, ‘Power analysis’).

As in the previous section, a fixed-effects meta-analysis of three studies that provided trait questionnaires specifically targeting beliefs about ability yielded no statistically significant results (both a priori networks |r| < 0.04, P > 0.511, BF10 < 0.07, uncorrected; k = 3, n = 444). No voxels survived thresholding; all Bayesian posterior odds favoured the null hypothesis (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.25).

As for trait questionnaires, there was no statistically significant association between average down-regulation of task-based affective ratings and average neural activity during reappraisal in the preregistered regulatory networks, with strong support for the null hypothesis by Bayes factors (both |r| < 0.03, P > 0.22, BF10 < 0.03, uncorrected; k = 31, n = 1,958). No voxels within these networks survived correction for multiple comparisons in voxel-wise analyses.

Within canonical emotion regulation networks2, about 98% of voxels showed null effects that were decisively supported by Bayesian posterior odds (mean = 0.00, range 0.00 to 0.29), with only 12 voxels falling into an indecisive range (mean = 0.84, range 0.34 to 2.52). By contrast, five voxels in the brainstem (caudal pons) provided substantial evidence for an effect (mean = 7.31, range 4.84 to 13.89). Using uncorrected Bayesian posterior odds, evidence for effects was observed in 55 voxels exceeding 3:1 odds, including the amygdala (mean = 69.63, range 3.02 to 1,055.27). This pattern aligns with the uncorrected preregistered findings from the amygdala region-of-interest analyses (see ‘Divergence of capacity indices’).

For whole-brain analyses, the jackknife procedure indicated that results were highly sensitive to the inclusion of data from Brehl et al.21 (Extended Data Fig. 4), potentially owing to its large sample size in combination with study-specific effects (for example, data were collected in the context of the first COVID-19 outbreak). In the full analysis, a negative association with task-based affective ratings was observed in a cluster of 86 voxels outside the canonical regulatory networks. Excluding data from Brehl et al.21 increased the extent of significant voxels substantially to 587, mainly in sensorimotor and dorsal attention regions, with smaller clusters in visual cortex, caudate nucleus and brainstem (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Table 1). Across these regions, better down-regulation of negative emotions was associated with lower activation (mean = −0.11, range −0.16 to −0.09). Together, these results suggest that classically emotion-generating regions, but not emotion-regulating regions, are indicative of emotion regulation capacity, albeit with small effect sizes.

To facilitate the psychological interpretation of the significant neural activation pattern, we conducted automated meta-analytic decoding using Neurosynth, which quantifies the association between whole-brain activation maps and large-scale term-based meta-analytic patterns derived from the neuroimaging literature (for example, ‘pain’, ‘fear’ and ‘motoric’). Neurosynth decoding against 50 topic maps from 11,406 fMRI studies indicated that the meta-analytic activation map is most similar to language processing (‘comprehension’: r = 0.17, ‘sentence’: r = 0.16 and ‘semantic’: r = 0.14) and most dissimilar to sensorimotor processing, consistent with the deactivation observed in whole-brain analyses (‘hand’: r = −0.25, ‘movements’: r = −0.22, ‘motor’: r = −0.17).

Top-down theoretical models predict that effective reappraisal should be associated with lower amygdala and higher prefrontal responses—an opposing pattern. Between-person differences in overall brain responsivity12,22, however, could blur such regional specificity.

Contrary to theoretical predictions, participants with stronger amygdala responses during reappraisal also showed substantially stronger responses throughout the rest of the brain in the same contrast (mean r = 0.27, range −0.08 to 0.68; Extended Data Fig. 5; correlation signs are reversed in the figures because amygdala down-regulation was coded as [view negative − reappraise negative]). This included both regulatory networks (first: r = 0.29, P < 0.001; second: r = 0.24, P < 0.001; k = 35, n = 2,088) and more than 170,000 voxels brain-wide, with only a single voxel showing a negative correlation (Fig. 2d). A person with a larger amygdala response than others, therefore, also tends to show larger responses in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and elsewhere—making the expected opposing pattern almost undetectable with standard fMRI individual-difference analyses.

This pattern was not unique to the amygdala. For all pairs among 489 anatomical regions23 (Methods, ‘Inter-region correlations’) in an independent reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33), any two brain regions were on average highly correlated across participants (r = 0.58, s.d. = 0.18).This means that individuals who respond more strongly in one region tend to respond more strongly everywhere across the brain, compared with other people. Crucially, this was not specific to reappraisal: the same pattern held across 18 studies spanning negative emotion, pain and cognitive control10 (mean r = 0.37; Fig. 3a), with between-person correlations among canonical resting-state network responses25 reaching 0.50–0.80 (Fig. 3b). Person-level whole-brain responsivity thus potentially reflects pervasive confounding processes for regional fMRI inference—an issue that affects not only reappraisal research, but also the broader task-based individual-difference literature.

a, Between-person correlations (that is, across participants) of regional activation across pairs of brain regions in an independent multimodal task–fMRI dataset spanning three domains—cognitive control, negative emotion and pain processing—with three subdomains per domain and two studies per subdomain (n = 15 per study; total n = 270). Each dot shows the mean Pearson correlation across all possible pairs of 489 regions; whiskers indicate the s.d. across region pairs. b, Between-person Pearson correlations of activation profiles between pairs of resting-state networks in the same dataset, additionally including a reappraisal dataset24 (n = 33). Colours encode the magnitude of Pearson’s r, and the top row shows the mean across studies. Networks were defined using the Yeo parcellation25. Rows show individual studies; columns show network pairs. dAttention and vAttention denote dorsal and ventral attention networks, respectively; Default denotes the default mode network.

These profound individual differences in global signal responses are in conflict with the argument that most fMRI tasks have been designed to elicit strong within-person effects, at the cost of meaningful between-person variance, despite their common use in individual-difference research26. We tested this potential misalignment by analysing trial-wise responses to negative pictures in two large samples with population-representative variance in negative emotional dispositions, using the most common reappraisal task12 (Methods, ‘Variance decomposition’). For trial-wise task-based affective ratings, the majority of variance was at the within-person level (92–93%; Fig. 4). By contrast, for neural responses in the amygdala and regulatory networks, about 60% of variance was on the between-person level. Thus, associations are likely to be reduced because common fMRI task designs prioritize robust within-person condition effects over between-person effects26, a mismatch that is further amplified by large individual differences in global signal responses.

Variance decomposition for three focal outcomes—task-based affective ratings, amygdala responses and regulatory network responses—in two large task–fMRI studies50 (the Pittsburgh Imaging Project (PIP) (study 1) n = 176, and Adult Health and Behavior Project, phase 2 (AHAB-2) (study 2) n = 180; Supplementary Table 1). Bars show the proportion of total variance attributable to between-person and within-person variability. Single-trial responses were extracted for each outcome and decomposed using intercept-only linear mixed-effects models, with the random intercept indexing between-person variance and the residual term indexing within-person variance. To obtain stable estimates, trial-level responses outside three times the interquartile range were removed within each participant, followed by removal of participants whose average responses fell outside three times the interquartile range. Between-person variance estimates were low for task-based affective ratings but substantially higher for amygdala and regulatory network responses. Exact proportions of total variance attributable to between-person differences were as follows. Study 1: ratings 0.07, 95% confidence interval [0.05, 0.09]; amygdala 0.64, 95% confidence interval [0.59, 0.69]; regulatory network 0.62, 95% confidence interval [0.57, 0.66]. Study 2: ratings 0.08, 95% confidence interval [0.06, 0.10]; amygdala 0.60, 95% confidence interval [0.55, 0.65]; regulatory network 0.56, 95% confidence interval [0.51, 0.61].

Finally, we tested whether multivariate neural signatures provide more sensitive indices of reappraisal capacity than anatomically defined regions or networks. Neural signatures are predictive decoding models that combine activity across many brain regions to estimate the presence or intensity of a psychological state in new individuals. We focused on three established candidate signatures: a negative affect decoder, a decoder of reappraisal as a dynamic state, and a decoder trained to predict individual differences in reappraisal success from task-based affective ratings (Methods, ‘Multivariate neuro-affective signatures’).

Using the four largest studies (n = 730), we first examined whether these signatures differentiated emotion generation from reappraisal (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Table 2). The negative affect decoder was strongly expressed during emotion generation (d = 0.69) but increased further during reappraisal (d = 0.15), indicating that its expression did not follow the expected reappraisal-related reduction in negative affect. The reappraisal state decoder showed stronger negative expression during emotion generation (d = −0.41) than positive expression during reappraisal (d = 0.30), suggesting limited specificity for reappraisal as opposed to variation in emotional state. The reappraisal ability decoder showed substantial negative expression across both contrasts (d = −0.22 for emotion generation and d = −0.37 for emotion regulation). Consistent with these ambiguous task-response profiles and univariate null findings, none of the three signatures was significantly associated with reappraisal capacity, whether indexed by trait questionnaires or task-based affective ratings (P > 0.08; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Table 3). Descriptive correlations were near-zero (|r| ≤ 0.06), with confidence intervals excluding effects larger than |r| = 0.15 and Bayes factors favouring the null hypothesis (BF10 < 0.25), especially for the negative affect decoder (BF10 < 0.09).

a, Responses of neural signatures, the amygdala and the regulatory network to the two main contrasts: emotion generation [view negative – view neutral] and emotion regulation (reappraise negative – view negative). Metrics are expressed as Cohen’s d. Smaller points indicate study-specific estimates; larger points and error bars indicate estimates aggregated across studies and their 95% confidence intervals (uncorrected, two-sided). Total n = 730; study 1 n = 180 (AHAB-250), study 2 n = 176 (PIP50), study 3 n = 139 (Doren et al., unpublished) and study 4 n = 235 (ref. 21). The negative affect decoder was not used in study 1, and the reappraisal ability decoder was not used in study 2 to avoid inflated effect sizes, as these were the training samples for the previously published decoders. For exact statistics, see Extended Data Table 2. b, Between-person Pearson correlations of the three neural signatures with trait questionnaires and task-based affective ratings. Smaller points indicate study-specific correlations; larger points and error bars indicate pooled correlations and their 95% confidence intervals (uncorrected, two-sided).
