#1218. Ballon d'Or Power Rankings: Why Harry Kane should win over Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe, and Lionel Messi

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The deadlines have passed, the votes have been tallied and verified, all that is left is to crown the outstanding male footballer of the 2025-26 season. That might be easier said than done.

Twelve months ago it was quite obvious that Ousmane Dembele would be taking home this prize. He had the narrative, he had the performances and he had the silverware. In years without major international tournaments it is often the case that being the best team on the Champions League winner is enough and so it proved for Dembele, who only really fulfilled the promise of a career in the back half of Paris Saint-Germain's breakout season. Mohamed Salah and Raphinha had cases based on individual performance but when it came down to medals, it really was hard to see past Dembele. He fulfilled all the criteria.

This time the very best performers of the club season did not take home that one extra trophy to buttress their campaign. Bayern Munich and Barcelona won their domestic leagues. Big whoop. The English champions almost exist as a counter to the individual qualities the Ballon d'Or glorifies. Arsenal won the league in spite of the absence of their star forwards, a triumph of depth and resilience that is unlikely to earn them many podium spots. Paris Saint-Germain repeated the league and Champions League double but half their strongest XI barely showed up in Ligue 1. Dembele can hardly repeat off around 2500 minutes for club and country last season.

As is always the case, the World Cup promises to warp voting. It clarifies little among the front runners. Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe had great individual tournaments but one of the Ballon d'Or's three criteria is "team performances and achievements". England and France fell short there. Lamine Yamal fulfills that, but Spain's triumph was one of the collective, the greatest prize in the sport won despite their forward struggling with injury.

Meanwhile, the best at the tournament do not sit easily in this ranking. Rodri might have held Spain together, but his domestic season was hampered by injury. Lionel Messi's historic standing was only buttressed by what he did as a 39-year-old, but your mileage may vary as to the significance of an MLS Cup-winning run beforehand.

This year more than most, then, there is no right answer. This, at least, is the least wrong I can offer. And we'll end this preamble with a customary reminder: this is not a prediction for who will win the Ballon d'Or. If you want that, consult your preferred sportsbook, I guess, or our own Golazo rankings. This is who ought to win it. You will probably disagree.

Perhaps it was the endings to his tilts at the Champions League and World Cup that make it so hard to lock in on Kane as the best player in the world last season. If the 33-year-old really were that good, would he not have found a way to bend the biggest games in his direction? That semifinal against Argentina in particular was one of those late-summer Kane games where he looks too leggy to impact the game either in the penalty area or the midfield roles he drops into, usually with such success.

That's one game though. There are another 64 where he was frequently spectacular. A remarkable 73 goals for club and country is the sort of output that belonged back in Messi's prime years. The absolute biggest game may not have gone his way but Kane was unforgettable against the Ivory Coast, thrilling in both legs against PSG and incisive in putting Real Madrid to the sword.

Then there are the Bundesliga numbers. Gaudy output is the baseline for a Bayern striker against domestic opposition but still the only players to have bettered Kane's 36 goals in 31 league games are Gerd Muller and Robert Lewandowski. The former won the Ballon d'Or, the latter probably would have if it had been awarded in 2020. There is no reason why Kane should not get it this time.

PSG were ultimately the best side in Europe last season and yet judging which of their players deserves the Ballon d'Or is a challenge. Ligue 1 might not demand much of them but it does feel unreasonable to reward a player who spent half his weekends watching on from the sidelines because his head coach can afford to save him for the trickier tests that come with retaining the Champions League. At some point there has to be a minutes restriction. If you're not seeing the pitch for half of your team's league minutes, then it is really hard to make a case for you to be one of the 10 best performers in the world last season. Either you were injured, unfortunate but still a disqualifying factor, or your team are not frequently playing opponents of a sufficient standard.

All of which is to say that Dembele, Joao Neves, Nuno Mendes and even you Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, you've got to go. Yes, you looked like some of the best players in the world in the spring. It's just that you had most of the autumn off.

As for Vitinha, there's a reason why he played nearly 4000 club minutes and only one other starter in the Champions League final cleared 3000. The Portuguese midfielder was the engine without which his side could not motor forward. Across Europe's top five leagues, he ranked third for progressive carries per 90 minutes and second for progressive passes. Unlike most tempo setters in midfield, he also weighed in with crucial goals and assists, firmly establishing himself as the best midfielder on the planet.

The sport's assist king last season. If we consider domestic cups and leagues, European matches and the World Cup, then Michael Olise ended the year with 10 more goals laid on for his teammates than anyone else. The summer definitively proved that he could be the lead attacker in a frontline made up of some of the best forwards in the world, but then again, his form with Bayern Munich had shown as much.

In general, when we're reflecting back on the season, we shouldn't lean too heavily on expected goals and assists. What we're really looking at is actual returns and if that meant a player was out over the skis, well, more power to them. Having said that, I mean, talk about separating yourself from the field.

In pure output terms, Yamal, still just 19 years of age, was perhaps a little off the peak of Europe's attackers, 37 goals and assists when Kane, Olise and Mbappe were all in the 40s or higher. Still, it was enough that a starring role in the World Cup might just have swung Yamal into top spot. Unfortunately, a biceps femoris injury put paid to the prospect of him showing more than flashes of his best self in the summer.

Unfortunately for Yamal, that was the story of his 25-26, where 96 days were lost to injuries that included a nagging groin issue in the autumn. That is among the most common problems faced by young footballers who are still growing into the bodies of seasoned athletes. On the evidence of when he was on the pitch, Yamal will be a Ballon d'Or winner when he has reached full physical maturity.

Here's maybe the trickiest candidacy to get a read on. In terms of goal contributions, only Kane beats him, and when the lights shone brightest at the World Cup, Mbappe was phenomenal. By the time he retires, likely with at least two more tournaments under his belt, his high watermark for World Cup scoring might look a bit like Michael Phelps' Olympic gold record or Wilt Chamberlain's scoring titles.

For an individual award, individual output really matters. If the Ballon d'Or were about team performance, then you would have the ludicrous scenario where Real Madrid campaigned for Dani Carvajal to win the prize in 2024 if Rodri was going to get it anyway. After all, he was there for the Euro 2024 win and the Champions League too. That'd be mad. Aaah.

However, team success is one of the criteria and it's one that needs to be at least partially weighed when you play for Real Madrid and France. You can't make the Russell Westbrook 2017 case for Mbappe. His goals and assists need to lead to something. In the summer they very nearly did.

A reminder once again that this is not a prediction. Gabriel Magalhaes probably is not going to make the top 10. The best odds you can find of him winning the Ballon d'Or are +6600, an implied probability of 1.5%. That's defenders and this prize, folks. Only three of them have won it in history. Franz Beckenbauer is the only one to have managed it without winning the major international tournament of that year.

There is a reason for that. The most valuable and difficult skill in this sport is scoring goals. In the era of three points for a win, attack tends to deliver the biggest prizes. That's what made Arsenal's Premier League win so remarkable. It and the near miss in the Champions League final were built on one of the most exceptional defenses in the history of this sport, anchored by the brilliant Gabriel, whose blend of skill and tenacity made him the best Arsenal player last season.

With shot-disrupting qualities that are Victor Wembanyama-esque -- 13.2% of shots Arsenal faced when Gabriel was on the field were blocked by their No. 6 -- the man the Emirates Stadium calls the king of Brazil made it far harder for the other team to do that most valuable and difficult thing on the pitch. It takes something special for a defense to carry an injury-riddled team to a league title. That Gabriel anchored that something special merits a very high place in the final voting.

Now, here's a weird one. As what might broadly be viewed as the third attacker on Bayern Munich, it's really hard to make a case for Luis Diaz winning the Ballon d'Or. Even he has been arguing that his teammate Kane should get it. "For me, he's number one to win it," Diaz said earlier this month. "Hopefully he gets it. We're trying to make his case to win it."

What we are really arguing here is that Diaz was so excellent in his particular role that it makes him one of the 10 best footballers in the world last season. With 39 goals and assists combined, it is not that hard a case to make. Diaz was also an exceptional passer, an outstanding creator for others and vital at moving Bayern into dangerous areas. There are players below him in this list who have more of a case to have been the best player in the world but really no one ranked sixth, seventh or eighth is actually going to win the Ballon d'Or. Consider this a reflection on how impactful Diaz was.

The inverse of a player such as Diaz might be Bruno Fernandes, who took a far inferior team on his back and propelled them to levels that they would not have gotten close to otherwise. When Fernandes started moving through the gears in the back half of the season, Manchester United flew from midtable to the Champions League.

Along with Gabriel, Fernandes is the player who tells the story of the great tactical trend of 2025-26 as well as anyone. Nine of his record-breaking 21 Premier League assists came from set pieces and for a time there might have been no attacking scenario more difficult to defend than Fernandes standing over a corner, lobbing it into a mass of bodies from which Casemiro would often rise the highest.

It wasn't just set pieces for Fernandes, whose 99 open-play chances created were 22 more than any other player in Europe's top five leagues last season. For a sense of just how impactful he was, one need only observe how United are struggling now that he has come back down to earth.

For these last two, the question really is how much importance you place on the World Cup. Obviously, it is the peak of the sport but what happens when you've spent the rest of your time playing at a level that ClubELO and Opta would consider to be a fair way below England's second tier, at or around the level of the Norwegian, Ecuadorian and Swiss domestic leagues? If you're as historically excellent as Messi, you're probably going to look sprightlier and more incisive than those who have spent the preceding nine months slogging their way through the Champions League and European domestic seasons.

If that sounds like a means of diminishing Messi's brilliance at the World Cup, it shouldn't be. Being the best player on the runners-up at 39 is an exceptional achievement, one that only serves to reinforce his status as the greatest of all time. It also should have resulted in him being named player of the tournament. The Ballon d'Or, however, is awarded for the period from Aug. 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026. For too much of that, Messi was playing at a level that was simply beneath his talents.

Somewhat as above, really. At the World Cup, Rodri was Rodri, the player who was so eminently worthy of winning the 2024 Ballon d'Or. When Spain had the ball, Rodri, now at Barcelona, was the man who moved them through the lines, who carried the ball almost as effectively as he passed it. When Spain didn't have the ball, Rodri got it back for them.

Flashes of that Rodri had emerged as he stepped up his recovery from an ACL injury in his final months as a Manchester City player. He was brilliant for a half against Chelsea in January, the best player on the pitch when City beat Arsenal in the EFL Cup final. Even Pep Guardiola, however, knew that the "real Rodri" would not emerge until later on in the season. That puts a hard cap on where he can rank.

#1216. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL

As the home fans set off flares, filling the air with plumes of thick, red smoke, the theme tune to Captain Pugwash was played. Arteta tried to find answers from his coaching staff, amid the cacophony, but occasionally you do not have to look too deep for answers.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Viktor Gyökeres gets his first goal of the season and Arsenal are level against Fleetwood! 🔴 https://t.co/LfZcIbAfCX

A game of attack against defence played out for the remainder before Dowman was harshly dismissed in the 85th minute after reacting to a tough challenge from Neal. There was still time for Fleetwood’s Lynch to make two excellent saves from White and Odegaard in added time as Arsenal tried to avoid the shoot-out lottery. They could not and how it hurt them.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ

“Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and removed,” Matt Lawlor, the Fleetwood manager, said. “To me, there was that feeling we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special.

“To be giving that to football fans and especially Fleetwood fans is unbelievably special. I’m really proud of it. Football’s a funny old game, isn’t it?”

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players. I haven’t seen anyone not doing what is required at this level. But, obviously, we insisted so much, we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, obviously, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t. And football is about that.

Attitude wise, absolutely zero [wrong] otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way. It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline.

Something that we discussed already before the match.

It’s difficult to see on the cameras, I prefer to watch it back properly and I will assess the situation.

We will learn from everything [on if he will learn from it].

I don’t think it will [sink in], it’s really hard to address the players when we have a league game on Saturday and I didn’t want to be the bearer of reality. The biggest night in the club’s history. We’ve beaten the champions, somehow!

We knew before the game, we’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to go to the best team in the country and the most organised team in the country and the best of the basics and the world-class players, in that we’re going to go and outplay them. So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them. And I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.

Obviously, the goal happens, but they’re going to happen; they’re so good at football. The footballers that they have, the gaps that they find and we see it every week in the Premier League.

To beat the English champions on penalties, credit to everyone one of these lads. We looked at Grimsby beating Man Utd last year. We compared it even though these are the champions. We thought ‘if we lay it all out there, let’s see what happens.

The team who are 18th in League Two have beaten the Premier League champions. Nine perfect penalties and one miss from Bruno Guimaraes.

Lynch dives to his left after the Guimaraes stutter, good save from the goalkeeper.

Arsenal are out if Haughey converts this penalty.

Cannon scores against Arsenal at Highbury. Bruno G up next.

Gyokeres finishes with power. The perfect record continues. Cannon up next for Fleetwood.

Meslier dives the wrong way again, Davies does well to keep his composure after needing a few attempts to spot the ball.

All four penalties have been scored, Havertz sends Lynch the wrong way after missing a few chances in regulation time.

Cracking penalty from midfielder, into the roof of the net with power.

Lynch guessed the right way, but Odegaard found the bottom-right corner with power.

He waits for Meslier to dive and rolls the ball into the opposite corner.

Odegaard is going to take first for Arsenal.

Their striker Coughlan, on as a sub in the second half, is going to take the first penalty of the shoot-out against Meslier.

Arsenal taken to penalties by the team 18th in League Two. They finish the game with a sense of injustice after Max Dowman’s red card, but they only have themselves to blame for not putting Fleetwood to the sword in the second half. Huge defensive effort from the underdogs.

Arsenal continue to pile the pressure on even with 10 men, but Guimaraes’s cross is claimed by Lynch.

Fleetwood then go on the attack, and White makes a mess of Rooney’s cross, conceding a cheap corner.

One last chance to win the tie, but Arsenal deal with it.

Havertz then heads the ball down in a dangerous zone but no Arsenal player is there. Arsenal have had their best spell since the red card, almost playing with some anger.

Brilliant save from Lynch to deny Ben White at the back post! Stopped right on the line, just as five minutes of stoppage time are shown on the board.

Then Lynch turns behind another Odegaard shot for a corner.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ

Bruno Guimaraes floats in a cross that is too heavy for Ben White. Fleetwood have a free-kick which they are going to send into the mixer but Arsenal clear.

Mikel Arteta did not have much sympathy for Dowman as he walked past him, but replays suggest it was a harsh call. No VAR in play tonight. Arsenal now playing with 10 for the final minutes.

I suspect Mikel Arteta will feel a little differently about this situation when he sees a replay of what actually happened. https://t.co/tflU7nc831

The Arsenal winger reacted to a heavy challenge, and the referee has judged that he kicked out. There was very little in the incident, a slight movement of his left leg rather than a full-on swing.

RED CARD for Max Dowman! 🟥 https://t.co/wq4EvRIScm

Fleetwood’s best attacking moment of the second half! White and Mosquera got themselves in a mess before Meslier made a smothering save from Davies. Havertz heads the resulting corner clear but Eze messes up a promising Arsenal break.

Arsenal continue to hog possession around the Fleetwood box, but since both teams made their subs, the home team have started to look more comfortable again. Eze’s shot is blocked, and then he is caught offside.

Arsenal making another couple of changes: Guimaraes and Konsa replace Lewis-Skelly and Zubimendi.

For Fleetwood: Davies replaces Loupalo-Bi.

Ben White caught offside just as Arsenal were building up a head of steam in attack. “Champion of England, you’re having a laugh” is the chant from the home fans.

From that Arsenal free-kick, Havertz’s low cross goes straight into the side-netting. The German has had a bit of a stinker, Arsenal will need better at Anfield on Sunday. I’m sure Arteta would have liked to have taken off Havertz or Gyokeres by now.

Haughey wins an important tackle on Lewis-Skelly after Arsenal found the free player in the box, and from the resulting short corner Dowman’s shot is straight Lynch.

Dowman is then hacked down by Batty, who was tempted in by a heavy touch. Booking for the Fleetwood defender.

If the game finishes level, we will go straight to penalties. One or two players on both teams with heavy legs, but Arsenal surely have to turn the screw from here.

Coughlan is an in-form striker who is trying to offer Fleetwood some more intensity and pressing from the front. Despite all that Arsenal pressure, Fleetwood have not gone under since conceding the equaliser.

Havertz hesitant after Odegaard picked out his run and split the Fleetwood defence again. Neither let fly with the shot from a tight angle, nor picked out a cutback. Two changes from Fleetwood: Evans and McClean off, Coughlan and Murphy on.

And a change from Arsenal: O’Neill off, replaced by Eze. O’Neill was one of Arsenal’s brighter starters.

Bodies on the line from Fleetwood to keep the scores level, first Havertz and then Lewis Skelly had shots blocked from a free-kick floated into the box. Fleetwood need to hope for a second wind from somewhere.

Odegaard with another delightful flicked pass, but Havertz could only poke the ball into the side netting. Should be doing better with that chance, he had half of the goal to aim at. Arsenal knocking on the door, feels like a second goal is coming.

Havertz’s rebound actually flicked off Bennett’s head, or else that was a certain goal. As you would expect, Fleetwood now finding it very difficult to get out of their half or establish any possession. The combination of Odegaard’s introduction, the tactical tweak and some choice words look to have done the trick.

Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Eberechi Eze are among the players stepping off the bus, so at the very least it will be a strong bench.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

There is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.

Monday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZN

Tuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.

A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.

There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.

#1212. Premier League Power Rankings: Manchester United falling fast; Tottenham Hotspur, Bournemouth rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight games into a campaign, patterns are supposed to emerge as teams begin to lock into midseason form. This season of the Premier League is no exception, except the pattern is a new one – expect chaos until further notice.

Several teams are experiencing a regression to the mean after rocky starts to the season, evidenced by the weekend's most notable games. Aston Villa are surging up the table after a 2-1 win over Manchester City, Bournemouth defeated Manchester United in style with a 3-0 triumph at Old Trafford and Tottenham Hotspur have gone from zero wins to two in a week, a 2-0 win at Chelsea their most impressive performance in months. Others are also putting their early season results behind them, but it feels like they are crashing back down to earth – Brentford were held to a 1-1 draw at Hull City, while Ipswich Town were unimpressive in a 1-1 draw against Nottingham Forest.

A fascinating theme is beginning to emerge along the way. It feels like there are more midtable teams than usual, even if some sit as high as seventh (someone has to, after all). Then there are those that seem like relegation contenders but are several spots above the drop zone because, somehow, there are that many teams worse than them. There's a frenetic feeling to the Premier League table and, by extension, the latest edition of power rankings but the show must go on.

Here's how each Premier League team is looking after the latest round of games.

Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton was not glamorous but the Gunners won't care. They're level on points with Manchester City and well-positioned to compete for the title, much as they have been all season.

Manchester City's short-lived grip on first place is gone after their defeat to Aston Villa, one that raises questions about their ability to go the distance in Enzo Maresca's first season in charge.

Liverpool are slowly but steadily figuring things out with Andoni Iraola at the helm, a 2-0 win over Brighton and Hove Albion their most impressive result yet. A top-four spot feels like a realistic aim for this season, even if they are not the finished product just yet.

Fabian Hurzeler's side played a fairly even game with Liverpool, so their stock should not drop too much but the Reds did map out a plan to neutralize their attack-minded tendencies, which might be something opponents borrow from in the coming weeks and months.

This is where the extreme midtable energy of the Premier League comes in – Chelsea were deeply unimpressive against Spurs, unconvincing at almost every turn. Most teams in England's top flight, though, are worse off so the Blues hang onto fifth for now but they will be worth keeping an eye on.

Between a 3-0 win over AC Milan in the UEFA Europa League and their triumph at Old Trafford, it has been a fun week to be a Bournemouth fan. Those wins are a sign that things are finally clicking – they might be 13th in the league but they rank third on expected goal differential, a signal that things were always trending in the right direction.

Aston Villa's slow start is officially a thing of the past, Unai Emery's side smartly outmaneuvering City to prove just that. They are officially a team on the rise.

Leeds United's unstylish but effective consistency means they continue to hang out in the top half of the table but playing even against an unimpressive Sunderland side is not the kind of thing a team earns plaudits for.

There's no reason Brentford should not target a top-half finish but much like Leeds above them, an even game against relegation contenders Hull City is not indicative of the team's overall qualities.

Manchester United really have their hearts set on scaling down the table as fast as they can, don't they? The Red Devils should be better than this but their mistake-prone nature continues to be costly.

A win over Coventry City is one thing but a victory at Chelsea is another. More specifically, it's the kind of thing that ensured Spurs would dig themselves out of their early season hole and perhaps sets them up for some more normal results in the short-term.

There is no shame in losing to the reigning champions but Everton did not make much of a dent in the match, the Toffees seemingly resigned to being permanent residents of the middle of the Premier League's table for the foreseeable future.

For all their faults, Fulham have done well enough to pick up the points expected of them, the latest coming in a win over Coventry City. Barely cracking 0.5 expected goals along the way, though, is not something to write home about.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the other shoe will drop for Hull City but it hasn't yet, especially after picking up a well-earned point against Brentford.

Add Nottingham Forest to the list of anomalies this season, sitting firmly in the relegation zone despite ranking fifth in the league on expected goal differential. Case in point – they tallied 2.29 expected goals to Ipswich's 0.46 but tied 1-1 anyway. Until they solve that problem, they are doomed to less-than-ideal spots on the table.

Ipswich were lucky to pick up a point against Forest but the early season success is a thing of the past for them, too.

Eighth-place Newcastle United seem to be riding their luck – they rank 19th in the league on expected goal differential – but creating a five-point cushion above the drop zone by way of a win over Crystal Palace counts for something.

Sunderland will value the point they picked up against Leeds but they are in the midst of an unexciting season, which is hardly a position of strength for a team in desperate need of points.

Palace will take some solace from the fact that they outplayed Newcastle but in their case, the results actually reflect their form.

Coventry were neck-and-neck with Fulham on expected goals in defeat but considering the Cottagers put up a paltry number, there's not much the newly promoted side can brag about.

It's happened again. Another season, another Manchester United crisis. No longer does the end of daylight savings time herald the harsh winter ahead. Instead, it is the boos that ring around Old Trafford as the United faithful turn their ire on the same owners, the same executives and the same players, well aware it will be a different coach that pays the price.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth was remarkable only for the sheer unremarkability of it. In the 74 years after their first meeting in the 1949 FA Cup third round, Bournemouth won three games against Manchester United. In the last two years they have won three games: all at Old Trafford, all 3-0. Freddie Kruger is treading the boards at the Theatre of Dreams.

Although maybe that analogy is not quite apt. After all, the one positive that you could say about a Krugerian nightmare is that it tends to be a one-and-done situation. No such luck if you happen to be a Manchester United supporter. Could any of them now believe that sacking Michael Carrick would fix anything about this club? They've tried the Eddie Howe-esque Premier League mainstay, the relentless winner a la Antonio Conte, the graduate of the Ralf Rangnick pressing academy in the mold of Julian Nagelsmann. Their shortlist only needs an ex-Ajax coach to sweep the quadrants of post-Sir Alex Ferguson ineptitude. Fred Grim to Manchester United? Well, doesn't that sound about right?

This is a club suffering under profound mismanagement, the sort that no one individual can marshal on their own. So there's plenty of blame to spread around. Let's start doing so, in reverse order of course. Gotta keep you on the page as long as we can. Build some suspense. Who might be top, you wonder? Well you probably know. But you know most every AAA movie is going to end with the hero triumphant. The joy is in the journey to the inevitable end point.

Now look, the soon to be former Manchester United manager is not without his faults, as Bruno Fernandes so robustly articulated after the 4-1 defeat in Como. There have been some very weird technical decisions here this season and a head coach with a scintilla of authority probably could have got this team to stop taking so many shots from outside the box. And yet did anyone at Manchester United genuinely think they'd unearthed the next great coach when they threw him the salvage our season post-Ruben Amorim job?

That Carrick did so much more than that, guiding United to Champions League qualification through a third-placed finish, spoke to his ability to keep things simple. He retained what had worked from his predecessor, tidied up some of the complexities of the formation and rode Bruno Fernandes' player of the season form as far as he could go. It is not his fault that United have not kicked on since. What had the 45 year old achieved in three seasons at Middlesbrough that suggested a coach who would do much more than what most coaches do, get a team to perform at or around its talent level?

Maybe when the stars align, when his team has a game a week and a fully fit squad he could achieve something better than the field but it is no more sensible to project out Carrick's future off the spring hot streak than it is to discount his coaching ability because he has struggled to cope with the first confluence of injuries, unfortunate results and player ill-discipline of his tenure.

Old Trafford seemed to have the right sense of it on Sunday. "It's Carrick you know," reverberated around the ground until the minute he was down the tunnel. Then it was both barrels for everyone else.

No one associated with Manchester United should apologize for having exacting standards. A well-run version of this club would make every decision based on improving their title-winning prospects either in the short or medium term. There should be no need to take the long way to the Premier League summit.

Having said all that, goodness it does not take much to send this club into a doom spiral of nostalgia and despair. When Lisandro Martinez served notice on Jason Wilcox and the hierarchy United had performed pretty well in defeat away to Atletico Madrid, a result that few in the Champions League field could credibly bemoan. Their form had wobbled but only a dodgy Erling Haaland goal had taken Manchester City past them and the last two Premier League results had been disappointing but not disastrous draws.

In short things were not going well but the difficulties were explicable. Up to the loss at the Metropolitano at least one of United's major problems was they had scored fewer goals than their expected goals (xG) for and conceded more than the xG value of their opponents shots. Their actual goal difference was minus-one, their expected goal difference was a shade under plus four. There's some heavy lifting being done in there by thrashing Ipswich Town and Sabah but the aggregate of a good team probably does contain a couple of thrashings as well as games where you play even against seemingly inferior teams like Fulham.

In short, just as United weren't as good as last season's rise to third place -- the defense started wobbling quite dramatically into the spring -- they aren't really as bad as 16th in the table, a point clear of the relegation zone might have you believe. A clear-eyed assessment both of the relative talent of United and the rest of the league would say that this is a good team vulnerable to a wobble. Just stay the course, keep calm in the dressing room and block out the noise.

But, of course... this is Manchester United we're talking about.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe certainly talked a good game when he finally got his hands on the sporting infrastructure at Old Trafford in February 2024, his $1.6 billion investment for around a quarter of the club affording him INEOS Group control of football operations at United. No longer would this be a club in hock to the first team head coach, the Ferguson way of thinking to be replaced by a brain trust that included the sporting director, "probably the recruitment guys" and, for reasons, the chief executive and Ratcliffe himself. "In modern football, you need to decide what's your path and stick to your path," the new minority owner insisted.

In the two and a half years since Manchester United's path has led them to: openly canvass the market for a replacement for manager Erik ten Hag, trigger an extension clause in his contract when they couldn't find anyone better, spend over $400 million outfitting the Dutchman with new players, sack him within four months, hire a coach in Ruben Amorim who had talked himself out of better jobs thanks to his insistence on playing a 3-4-3, finish 15th, sack Amorim just as their analytical profile was on an upswing because he had fallen out with his employers, bring in Carrick temporarily and then permanently, spend almost all their budget on midfielders, get dragged in public by Martinez.

That's just the condensed lowlights. It's fair to say that you don't hear much any more about Project 150, the ambitious vision to mark a century and a half of the club with a 21st top flight title. Perhaps by 2028 sporting director Wilcox will have got round to fixing the defense having blown so much of the 2025 summer budget on attack before then spending nearly $200 million on a midfield that needed upgrades but got Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba while the left back spot was left untouched.

It would say everything about the cataclysmic mismanagement at a senior level if Wilcox -- like so many at the club a man with little top level experience of the role he has been thrust into -- gets the man said to be his preferred choice to succeed Carrick, Eddie Howe.

The same Eddie Howe who spent a hugely successful two years with Dan Ashworth at Newcastle United. The same Dan Ashworth who Manchester United spent £4.1 million on the poaching of and, five months later, firing of. The same Manchester United who in INEOS' period running the show rank ninth in the Premier League for points, 10th for expected goal difference. Still, at least they sacked staff and cut costs. Who ever could have imagined that as a fix for a business' problems?

Speaking after Sunday's 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, Harry Maguire pulled no punches. "At the moment it's nowhere near good enough and something needs to change," he said. He's not wrong. And yet the only constants at this club sit second and first in our rankings. Cast your mind back to the 4-0 thrashing at the hands of Brentford in August 2022, Erik ten Hag's second game in charge and oh, what, half a dozen crises ago. The starting back four for Manchester United on that Saturday evening in west London? Diego Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw. The starting back four in draws against Fulham and Everton more than four years later? Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw.

There are players at this club who have seen off half a dozen permanent managers. Some might not have lasted that long but in their time they have been frozen out or put up for sale. Few have paid the price for inconsistency. Why would you respect the authority of the head coach if you have spent three or four years in the Old Trafford dressing room and seen so many cycle through without any apparent accountability for the playing staff. It seems notable that Cristiano Ronaldo's bombing out by Ten Hag was followed by one of the most impressive runs of results in the last half decade. Players discovered their actions had consequences and started playing like that.

Now, they talk like they are bulletproof. Imagine Martin Odegaard used a post-match interview to mouth off about Mikel Arteta's tactics. Would he ever play for Arsenal again? That's a question Mesut Ozil and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang can answer. When a player did not perform for Pep Guardiola's Manchester City, he was swiftly sold. Meanwhile United's squad is preserved in aspic. Their defense moves like it is.

These are not players who lack for talent. United's first choice attack rivals any bar Manchester City and Liverpool. Their midfield needs careful construction to mitigate for its lack of pace but it has quality. When the mood takes them Maguire, Martinez and Shaw are perfectly solid defenders. As the graphic above suggests, this is a team that can have moments of extreme competence. That is how United got to third a few months ago. Were they helped by the coach's tactics or the hierarchy's recruitment? Not really but that does not make these expensive, well-remunerated players innocent bystanders, unable to arrest the decline.

More than two decades after Malcolm Glazer loaded debt onto Manchester United to fund his purchase of the club, what has been accomplished beyond a steady degradation of this behemoth of English culture. Being owned by the Glazers, who have not put any money into the club since the takeover, is estimated to have cost the club at least $1.5 billion, much of it spent on servicing debt from the initial takeover. It should be noted that 15 major trophies have been won in the time the Glazers have owned the club but 10 of them came in the period where Ferguson's sheer magnetism held the club together.

There is an argument to be made that United's commercial income skyrocketed under current ownership and certainly this was a club that was among the first to realize that every region could have its own bespoke set of sponsors, that there was always another billboard or patch on the jersey to splash with a logo. Those brands were not, however, flocking to United because of anything the Glazers had done. United were the dominant force in English football at just the right moment to benefit from the Premier League moving from national to global obsession.

Far from custodians, the Glazers are the most deleterious of landlords. An extractive force, they provide minimal service and value while taking their management fees, dividends, repayments and then the riches Ratcliffe paid for a slice of the pie. All of their money could have gone into retaining United's preeminence in the English game or at least staving off the impact of their indifference. As if to make the metaphor particularly on the nose, on their watch Old Trafford has decayed such that the cost of renovation, an estimated $1.6 billion, might just make a case for the planned new stadium that no supporter seems to want.

A club that even in fallow years ranks among the top 10 revenue generators in football has found itself on a cost-cutting drive for which Ratcliffe is the face both because the Glazers' debt acts as a competitive drag and because ownership showed no interest nor aptitude in improving the on-field product. If the players represent a culture that is accountability-lite then it is ownership that enables it. When we start this piece by warning that nothing will change post-Carrick it is because we have seen enough to know that nothing changes until those who tolerate this degradation of Manchester United are no longer in a position of power.

#1208. Wesley Fofana’s Chelsea nightmare continues as Liverpool win shoot-out

Unfortunately for Chelsea, Wesley Fofana put his hand up twice. Firstly to concede the first-half penalty for handball that allowed Liverpool to equalise quickly after Chelsea themselves had scored from the spot.

And secondly to volunteer to take one of the penalties in the shoot-out. The defender had to score to keep Chelsea in it, but he woefully, nervously skied his effort high into a gleeful Kop and it was Liverpool who went through to the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

LIVERPOOL ARE THROUGH TO THE QUARTER-FINALS OF THE CARABAO CUP! 🔴 Wesley Fofana blazes over to hand Liverpool their FIFTH consecutive victory ✅ https://t.co/M4n01R8DSk

There the reward for Andoni Iraola, the head coach, is a home tie against the club he left in the summer: Bournemouth. The draw has opened up for Liverpool, and they know it, with only Manchester City left of the other big guns. But despite again playing at Anfield, they would have preferred not to face such a dangerous and motivated opponent, who have just reeled off five wins and five clean sheets in a row under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose.

This was also a big win. A meaningful win. One that was celebrated as such with Dua Lipa’s One Kiss – an anthem on Jürgen Klopp’s run to Liverpool’s first Champions League final under him in 2018 – played over the loudspeakers at the end as the players joyfully milled around the pitch.

One kiss is all it takes 🎶 https://t.co/0jfujy4V94

“I am happy to feel it. We feel the support,” Iraola said when asked whether he sensed the momentum and togetherness building in his reshaped Liverpool side. It looks as though they are.

Fofana was Chelsea’s eighth taker, so they were running out of options, but it was a truly terrible effort. The 25-year-old turned and scratched his head – just as many Chelsea fans have done over his underwhelming, albeit injury-hit, contributions since his eyebrow-raising £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

Both sides had the chance to win it earlier in the shoot-out. For Liverpool it was Kostas Tsimikas, who had taken the decisive kick to beat Chelsea in a shoot-out in the 2022 FA Cup final, but the Greek full-back also completely missed the target.

Tsimikas has the chance to put Liverpool through... And fires over the bar! 😱 https://t.co/eCKBT6njMB

Then Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha – on his debut – saw his kick saved, after an effort by Ryan Gravenberch had also been stopped. In the end, Liverpool’s stand-in captain Joe Gomez – still to score an actual goal – crashed in his kick before Fofana’s blunder. The 29-year-old Gomez finally “scored” and it was an assured strike.

This was the fifth penalty shoot-out between these two clubs, in all competitions, with Liverpool having now triumphed in all five. They won the toss for this one and elected to take the kicks in front of the Kop, which roared its satisfaction and did its best to unsettle the Chelsea takers.

Both stand-in goalkeepers – Giorgi Mamardashvili and Mike Penders – made one outstanding save each in the shoot-out. Chelsea substitute Valentín Barco was the other player to miss, hitting a post.

Chelsea blink first in the shootout! 🔵 Valentín Barco's penalty bounces off the post... https://t.co/rSXGfQctbI

The other efforts, in truth, were outstanding and assured with Liverpool, undoubtedly, benefitting from Iraola turning to his bench and bringing on Alexander Isak, Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola. All scored their penalties.

Among Chelsea’s scorers was Jordan Henderson and the former Liverpool captain received a strange homecoming in his first appearance at Anfield for three years. He was booed, in the first half at least, and especially when he tucked the ball under his arm before Chelsea took their penalty – in normal time – which gave them the lead. Henderson turned to the stands, grinning.

Morgan Rogers buries the spotkick! ⚽️ Chelsea take the lead at Anfield 🔵 https://t.co/YlDn2gakRi

Afterwards, Alonso faced more questions about his decision not to use Estêvão Willian. That is a gift from Chelsea. The communication at the back between Gusto and Fofana is poor, with the former playing a poor pass backwards looking for Fofana, who cannot reach it and the ball rolls behind for the easiest of corners for Liverpool in front of The Kop.

Gakpo takes an outswinging corner but Welbeck is on hand to head away at the front post.

We are yet to see the first goal of the night at Anfield but they are flying in at the Stadium of Light. Brentford have pulled a goal back against Sunderland through Callum Wilson and it is now 3-1 in the north east.

Chelsea want a penalty. Rogers goes down inside the Liverpool penalty area under a challenge from Araujo but it was a fair shoulder-to-shoulder challenge and that is not a penalty.

At the Stadium of Light, Sunderland are in dreamland. Malick Fofana has put them 3-0 up against Brentford closing in on half-time.

A wasted free kick from Chelsea, and goodness, Austin McPhee is not happy. Chelsea’s set piece coach was up on the touchline, remonstrating to nobody in particular but it was obvious to see the frustration that the plan he has worked on - a chip to the side, a cutback into the middle - has fallen down at the first attempt. To compound his fury, McPhee just blew a gasket after Chelsea were not awarded a penalty following a coming together between Ronald Araujo and Morgan Rogers.

Tsimikas has let Ngumoha down there. Ngumoha does brilliantly to dribble through two Chelsea defenders around the halfway line and drives down the left. He then plays the ball outside to Tsimikas, who should do so much better with his cross but picks out the front-post defender Lacroix.

Meanwhile at Craven Cottage, Crystal Palace have taken the lead at Fulham thanks to Eddie Nketiah.

McConnell becomes the second Liverpool player to be booked tonight for handball. He lost the ball on halfway and cynically handled the ball as Rogers attempted to counter. A fairly clear-cut booking for McConnell there.

A reminder that there is no VAR tonight and if the game is level after 90 minutes, we will go straight to penalties. Referee Darren England has summoned Chelsea captain Caicedo and former Liverpool midfielder Henderson over for a word.

Caicedo puts Tsimikas’ cross from the left behind for the first corner of the night. Gakpo sends in the inswinger but the whistle goes as Chelsea are awarded a free-kick for a foul from Tsimikas on Gusto.

There has yet to be a goal at Anfield but at the Stadium of Light Sunderland have doubled their lead over Brentford courtesy of Tymur Tutierov’s goal.

The first booking of the night at Anfield goes the way of the home side. Koumas slides in to try and block a clearance from Lacroix and is booked. Koumas barely touched Lacroix and that is never a yellow card.

Meanwhile, in the north east, Sunderland have taken the lead against Brentford through Chemsdine Talbi.

Brighton had led in Manchester but the home side have just equalised. Mateo Kovacic has scored from range to bring Manchester City level with five minutes to go in the first half.

Clear to see in these early exchanges that Cody Gakpo has been deployed as Liverpool’s main “striker” with Lewis Koumas, James McConnell - who played in the 2024 final when Liverpool beat Chelsea 1-0 - and Rio Ngumoha operating in behind him. Jordan Henderson seems to be the man whom Xabi Alonso wants to trigger Chelsea’s press. They are playing a rigid 4-5-1 formation but, this being Alonso, the system is always flexible. His ethos is to be able to play two or three systems in a game if needed.

Ngumoha drives at Neto down Liverpool’s left and is felled by the Portuguese forward. It is an obvious free-kick and Neto is a touch fortunate not to be booked for that blatant foul. Ngumoha, who was fantastic for Liverpool against Villarreal in the Champions League just over a week ago, already into the action.

Tsimikas clips in the delivery but it is headed away by Lacroix.

The second goal in the League Cup this evening has come in Manchester and has gone the way of the away side. Malick Yalcouye has put Brighton in front against Manchester City on the half-hour mark.

We are under way at Anfield. Who will book their place in the League Cup quarter-finals; Liverpool or Chelsea?

Jordan Henderson is busily going around geeing up Chelsea’s players, in exactly the same fashion as he did when he played in this stadium for 12 years. He got an ovation here in May, when Brentford drew 1-1, that left him extremely emotional but it remains to be seen what will happen when he gets his first touch this evening. There has been no acknowledgement - yet - from The Kop and the same is true for Xabi Alonso. But, then again, why would there be when there is such lingering enmity between these clubs?

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at Anfield. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Liverpool: Mamardashvili; Araujo, Gomez, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; McConnell, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Gravenberch, Gakpo; KoumasSubstitutes: Alisson, Endo, Jacquet, Wirtz, Isak, Mac Allister, Chiesa, Barcola, Chambers.

Chelsea: Penders; Acheampong, Lacroix, Fofana, Gusto, Caicedo, Lavia, Henderson, Neto, Welbeck, Rogers.Substitutes: Sharman-Lowe, Colwill, Subuloye, Palestra, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao, Quenda, Emegha.

Has come on the south coast, where Bournemouth have taken the lead against Aston Villa courtesy of Amine Adli’s goal inside the opening 10 minutes.

“The cups are important for us this year. For sure, we face today a good challenge, coming to Anfield, and we want to be in the next round. It is another competition. We know it is another format, it is make-or-break, so we want to make it happen today with a great performance.

“From the beginning we have taken it seriously. We have a tough game and we want to have a good feeling that we are competing. We have to do many great things. In one game there can be many little games with the energy created. These players have played here before. We have practiced penalties but sometimes it is about the feeling of the day.”

The games at the Vitality Stadium, Craven Cottage and the Stadium of Light have just begun. That means four of the five ties tonight have started, with just the game at Anfield to begin in just over 10 minutes.

At The Etihad, Manchester City have kicked off against Brighton. Then, there are three 7.45pm kick-offs before Liverpool begin against Chelsea at Anfield at 8pm.

More than two years have passed since Rio Ngumoha chose to leave Chelsea for Liverpool, but the frustration remains at Stamford Bridge. The pain of losing a player of Ngumoha’s potential does not pass quickly, especially as the winger was part of Chelsea’s academy system for eight years. It must sting to see a London boy, one of their own, now delighting the Anfield crowd.

For many at Chelsea, the anger at Ngumoha’s departure in 2024 will probably never subside. Or, at least, it will not subside while he continues to develop so thrillingly at Liverpool. Such was Chelsea’s annoyance at the time of his exit, Telegraph Sport reported last year, Liverpool’s scouts were subsequently banned from attending matches at their academy centre.

Xabi Alonso spent five years as a player at Anfield between 2004 and 2009. He has returned twice as an opposition manager, with both ending in defeats; one as Bayer Leverkusen boss and one as Real Madrid manager.

It is an all-Premier League tie at Anfield as Liverpool host Chelsea in the last 16 of the League Cup, with a place in the quarter-finals at stake. This will be the first managerial meeting between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso.

Liverpool beat Tottenham 3-1 at Anfield in the last round of this competition, which included a stunning goal from Dominik Szoboszlai to seal progression to the last 16. They earned their first home Premier League win of the season on the weekend as they beat Brighton 2-0. Iraola’s men come into this game off the back of four straight wins in all competitions.

“There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game and we want to be competitive,” Iraola said ahead of this tie. “We have to see how the legs; we are not just in the Carabao Cup, but also in the Champions League and we have been trying to make changes from game to game. We want to be in the next round. We have been unlucky in the draw, playing Chelsea, and they have been unlucky also. But we want to be in the draw again and that only happens if you win. We need to rotate, all the top teams need to rotate when you are playing every three days. Sometimes you are forced to rotate due to injury or sometimes different demands in different games tactically. I am happy that everyone is involved. When we have had to use someone who has not played a lot of games, they have helped us. The more players we have in a good place, the easier my selection will be, even if it is hard to leave players out.”

Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitike remain long-term absentees for the hosts with Jeremie Frimpong also missing. Florian Wirtz could feature despite going off with an ankle knock during the win over Brighton.

Like Liverpool, Chelsea also had an all-Premier League tie in the third round of this competition, beating Leeds 6-3 in a high-scoring affair at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea come into tonight’s game off the back of a 2-0 defeat against Tottenham in the league last weekend. Not only did they lose on Saturday but to make matters worse for them Cole Palmer was sent off. As a result of that red card, Palmer is suspended for tonight’s tie.

“We [Alonso and Palmer] spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made,” Alonso said. “Things that you can avoid. I hope that this is not going to be repeated. He is aware of that, he is mature and it was a mistake. He is in a good space, he connects very well socially with his teammates. They like him, they want Cole smiling, they want Cole having fun, enjoying his game because when we see that, he will have a better team. I will just ask you because he has got this very cool persona, you probably know his personality is very interesting.”

Former Liverpool midfielder and current Chelsea boss Alonso has lost his two games as a manager against Liverpool; a 4-0 defeat as Bayer Leverkusen boss and then a 1-0 loss when in charge of Real Madrid, with both taking place at Anfield. Alonso is not the only ex-Liverpool midfielder to return to Anfield tonight as their former captain Jordan Henderson is in the Chelsea squad for tonight. Joao Pedro has missed the trip to Anfield because of a thigh injury which could rule him out for a few weeks.

The Premier league fixture between these sides at Anfield ended in a 1-1 draw back in May. In that match, Arne Slot was in charge of Liverpool with Calum McFarlane in interim charge of Chelsea. Chelsea won the reverse fixture 2-1 at Stamford Bridge. Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1205. Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

a, Distribution of number of distinct alleles per locus. b, Distribution of mode allele per locus. c, Distribution of summed alleles (of a diploid genotype). X-axis truncated at 100 repeats. Overall, 13.7% of alleles represented expansions relative to the locus-specific mode, 9.3% were contractions, and the remainder matched the mode allele exactly. The median summed dosage across all loci was 14 repeat units. Following stringent filtering for call quality and locus-level metrics (Methods), the resulting high-confidence callset had a median of 6 distinct alleles per locus and a median mode allele length of 9 repeats.

Bulk eTR catalogs were based on GTEx11,36 (bulk RNA-seq of whole blood; FDR < 10% for STRs and <5% for VNTRs) and gEUVADIS96 (bulk RNA-seq of HapMap lymphoblastoid cell lines; FDR < 5%) datasets. Differences in cell type/tissue resolution, TR genotyping methods, and analysis pipelines limit interpretability of direct comparisons. In particular, cell type-specific signals discovered in TenK10K Phase 1 may be diluted in bulk tissue, and TR catalogs used in prior studies may not capture loci genotyped in TenK10K Phase 1.

Distributions of sc-eTR effect sizes stratified by MANE gene annotation (a), ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory element (cCRE) annotation (b), and motif length (c). Violin plots show the distribution; centre lines indicate medians, boxes indicate interquartile ranges (IQRs), and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. MANE annotations: 5′ untranslated region (5′ UTR), coding sequence (CDS), and 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR). Unadjusted P values were calculated using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests (n = 112,100 sc-eTRs). In a, **P = 3.4 × 10−7 and *P = 1.6 × 10−4; in b, **P = 2.5 × 10−3 and *P = 3.1 × 10−3; in c, ***P = 6.1 × 10−9, **P = 2.6 × 10−7, and *P = 5.0 × 10−6.

UMAP plots of B cells (n = 539,820 cells) first labeled by cell identity, then subsequently labeled by low (15th percentile), medium (between 15th and 85th percentile) and high (above 85th percentile) activity scores for cell functions of natural killer cell activation, response to multicellular organisms, and protein localization to membrane. Swarmplots demonstrate a cell state-specific poly(TTTG) sc-eTR associating with SYNGR1 expression across the natural killer cell activation axis in n = 1,925 individuals. Horizontal bars indicate the first quartile, median, and third quartile. P values were calculated using two-sided Wald tests of the regression coefficient (β) and are uncorrected for multiple testing.

For each scenario, from left to right: brief description of the scenario, association swarm plots for the lead TR in each of the two cell types (n = 1,925 individuals; horizontal bars indicate the first quartile, median, and third quartile), association plots of all tested variants around the gene, with signals for both cell types overlaid. P values were calculated using two-sided Wald tests of the regression coefficient (β) and are uncorrected for multiple testing. The bar chart at the end summarizes each scenario at the level of eGenes, using the maximum from all pairwise cell type comparisons. Box templates created in BioRender; Tanudisastro, H. https://BioRender.com/avk16r9 (2026).

Swarmplots use scRNA-seq data (n = 1,925 individuals), scATAC-seq data (n = 922 individuals), and PacBio long-read sequencing methylation data (n = 25 individuals). Horizontal bars indicate the first quartile, median, and third quartile. P values were calculated using two-sided Wald tests of the regression coefficient (β) and are uncorrected for multiple testing. Longer summed repeats at this TR locus are associated with decreased gene expression, decreased chromatin accessibility, and increased methylation. Plots reproduced from ref. 60, CC BY 4.0.

a, Linkage disequilibrium (LD) between lead TRs or single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and their next most significant neighboring SNV within ±100 kb of the gene body, in the best-powered cell type (n = 13,093 genes). Violin plots depict the distribution of LD, highlighting median values (white horizontal bar), interquartile ranges (IQR; boxes indicate 25th to 75th percentiles), and whiskers extending to ±1.5×IQR. Lead TRs are grouped into equal-sized bins based on the number of distinct alleles genotyped. b, Functional enrichment of candidate causal sc-eTRs (n = 1,490 TRs) relative to all genotyped TRs. Observed log2 fold enrichment (center point) is shown with 95% confidence intervals. CDS, coding sequence.
