#1171. What's wrong with Kai Havertz and can he fix it in time for Liverpool vs. Arsenal showdown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If last season's visit to Anfield taught Arsenal anything, it was the need for a killer in the final third to break the game open. Fail to do so and they are vulnerable to the sort of magic that bamboozled them in August of last year, even if the man who scored that brilliant free-kick winner, Dominik Szoboszlai, is a doubt for Liverpool on Sunday.

And if this game is indeed one that will be decided by what Mikel Arteta terms the "moments players," then it could scarcely have come at a worse time for the Arsenal manager. Bukayo Saka -- the Gunners' top shot taker, goal scorer and expected goals compiler -- has more than a month left on the sidelines with the thigh injury he suffered in Munich. Noni Madueke could miss the trip with an ankle injury. Christos Tzolis has returned to training but has not played for his new club in more than a month. Max Dowman, the precocious youngster whom Arteta has already entrusted with turning the tide on Merseyside, will serve the first of a three-game ban for his controversial red card.

It speaks to the depth at Arteta's disposal that, even if none of the aforementioned quartet play, there will still be game changers in the side. Even so, this does feel like an occasion where a first-choice center forward in top form would be handy. Kai Havertz is not that. Twelve games in and this has been perhaps the weirdest season of all since this esoteric forward landed on English soil in 2020. At his best, he has blown his former club Chelsea away. His worst, meanwhile, includes a wasteful performance in the EFL Cup defeat at Fleetwood and a baffling new tendency to slip offside.

The obvious answer when a player slides from peak to trough in a matter of weeks is to consult his injury record. Havertz did return from the last international break early after straining a muscle and went straight back into the side, playing an hour against Leeds and featuring in every other game since. In those six games he has no goals and one assist. In most of the minutes he has played, he has struggled to link the Arsenal attack together the way he usually does, let alone to threaten the opposition goal. That is not, however, a hangover from his injury travails.

"There's nothing to do with that," said Arteta. "It's true that in terms of the numbers, we have dropped those numbers but he certainly had the chances as well to play."

That was the case against Fleetwood, seven shots for the German adding up to 0.72 expected goals. That sounds perfectly adequate on first pass, and there are certainly others in the Arsenal side who ought to have asked more of a League Two defense. And yet when chasing a game for 70 minutes, is it fair to ask for more than three-quarters of an xG from the senior attacker of the English champions, a man who has scored in two Champions League finals?

Wanting a bit more has been a familiar experience for both Chelsea and Arsenal during his time with them. For the Gunners, it has been over two and a half years since they discovered just how good Havertz could be for them. The shift to center forward in a 3-1 win over Sunday's opponents, Liverpool, was the start of a brilliant year leading the line. Across 37 Premier League games, the Germany international delivered 18 goals and nine assists, not Erling Haaland numbers but exceptional output for the center forward in Arteta's everyone-eats offense.

Even since that brilliant run, there have been flashes. For an hour in May's Champions League final, Havertz was as threatening an attacker as anyone in PSG colors. A few weeks earlier he had been excellent in defeat to Manchester City, not the first time he had bossed Arsenal's title rival. If Chelsea have the misfortune of running into their former star, they're probably going to get him in the mood to do some damage. Of all the attackers available to Arteta this week, Havertz is the nearest he has to a big-game hunter. Indeed, if you want to make the case against Arsenal "just signing a striker" in January (you shouldn't), a key component of your argument ought to be how few players suit this manager as well as a fully fit Havertz. It is just that, well, a fully fit Havertz has been an elusive creature. And yet if Arteta will not use injuries as justification for the current wobble, perhaps we shouldn't. And wobble this is. Through eight league games, Havertz is averaging fewer shots, goals and non-penalty xG than in any other season in his Arsenal career on a per-90 basis. The same is true when you adjust for the fact that the 27-year-old is touching the ball a bit less on average this season than last. There is one notable stat where Havertz's numbers have skyrocketed, though, and that is in offsides. In every Premier League season before this one, he was caught out behind the opposition defense on less than one occasion per 90 minutes. In most of them, he averaged around one offside per two full games played. This year, however, no one in the league matches Havertz's 10 offsides already, and the gap is not particularly close. Joint-second on seven are his teammate Bukayo Saka and Dominic Calvert-Lewin of Leeds.

Now, the sample size of minutes is still small and open to distortion. It might be that one explanation for Havertz's skyrocketing offsides is that he has played Aston Villa and their occasionally effective, invariably cavalier high line. Equally, not all of those 10 offsides are about what the defense did well or about a run that came at just the wrong moment from the center forward. Watch Havertz move a good moment too soon to collect a pass off his friend and captain Martin Odegaard before bending well wide from a promising shooting position against Villa, and you see what looks like a forward who is simply off color, nothing more and nothing less, really. Sometimes the easiest explanation is the correct one. Havertz is just a bit out of sync with both his game and that of his teammates, as his manager acknowledged on Friday.

"That kind of form and that kind of efficiency with the front players, it's very common," said Arteta. "Full trust on him and what he's doing."

The natural response, then, for Arteta would be to pick the next cab off the rank, as he did in the win over Everton where Viktor Gyokeres started. That was the Swede's best game of the season, but he still did not register a shot. Gyokeres scored against Fleetwood but took only two other shots. Per 90, he averages 0.92 shots, 16th on Arsenal, with both left backs ahead of him. The evidence of his past entanglements with elite opposition suggests that Gyokeres is not the player to turn to at Anfield.

Instead, it will be Havertz, in need of something of a jump-start to his season. While he retains the "full trust" of a manager who has never faltered in his support, there might be time enough to sniff out his best form.

#1167. MLS reveals 2027 sprint season schedule ahead of shift to European calendar

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While the MLS regular season has yet to come to a close, the details of the sprint season have now been released. The sprint season is a critical bridge to the league moving to a European calendar, as the 2027 season will take place under a condensed schedule in order to prepare for that. Each team will play 14 regular season matches, with one home and one away. The regular season will run from February 19, with Inter Miami and FC Cincinnati kicking things off, until Decision Day on May 8t, when there's a Hudson River Derby between New York City FC and New York Red Bulls to close out the season. With NYCFC set to open a new stadium in Queens, this should also be the final MLS game played at Yankee Stadium, which NYCFC have called home since joining the league in 2015. Truly the end of an era that went on for far too long.

Ahead of the shift, MLS wants to ensure that each week has a marquee matchup to highlight the best of what the league has to offer. There will also be another season of the Walmart Saturday Showdown and of Sunday Night Soccer, so that the biggest games of the week get their due credit. With stars from abroad such as Antoine Griezmann, Lionel Messi, Thomas Muller, and Evander pitting against young stars such as Cavan Sullivan, Julian Hall, Adri Mehmeti, and Peyton Miller, there's plenty to showcase as MLS prepares for a new era.

It’s an all-out sprint. 👀The 2027 MLS Sprint Season Schedule is here. ⬇️✏️: https://t.co/5qDlJnxjeW pic.twitter.com/71brwLBgcV

The top eight teams in each conference will qualify for the playoffs, with each round being played in a single-elimination format. That schedule is yet to be announced, but it will see a shift from the current format, where the eighth- and ninth-placed teams play a single-elimination wild card match prior to the first round being a best-of-three series. That playoff format has seen criticism due to being too long, so the sprint season does offer an opportunity to take a look at other formats ahead of a return to a standard schedule in the fall. Still, using playoffs will ensure that all five Concacaf Champions Cup spots are accounted for before the teams also return to full participation in the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open Cup

This split will help get MLS onto the same transfer market as the rest of the world. MLS doing their primary transfer window in the winter has long been an issue due to teams not being able to send players to America. It also could mean that MLS sides won't be pressured to sell their best players midseason, either with the summer transfer window being an enticing time for teams to wade in and get new players during their own preseason. The change will bring geographic challenges such as dealing with harsh winters, but those are no different from the thunderstorm and extreme heat risks that the league already faces during the summer months in such varied climates. With the shift also including teams stopping play for international breaks, it will also end the need to play without your best players available, which increases the quality in the league.

Following the conclusion of this sprint season, the 2027-28 MLS Season will kick off in July of 2027. It will then conclude with the MLS Cup playoffs, which will run until May of 2028, similarly to when most European leagues wrap up.

#1165. Manchester United's players, not Michael Carrick, should shoulder the blame after embarrassing loss to Chelsea

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Manchester United players have been at great pains in recent weeks to point out how they have been failed by the powers that be, by those with supposedly more influence than the 11 lads on the field. On occasion, you could argue they had the measure of the situation. There's just one little note for Lisandro Martinez, Bruno Fernandes and anyone else who counts themselves among the Old Trafford mutineers.

If you're going to start demanding greater professional standards from your employers, you would be well advised to hold yourself to the same level. It would be a real problem if, for instance, you earned yourself two yellow cards in the space of 210 seconds, handing your opponents the penalty from which they win the game. Sympathy will be in quite short supply for those who complain about the head coach's tactics or the sporting director's recruitment but then, when the circumstances are right, fail to exploit prime opportunities.

Lisandro Martinez was right when he intimated a fortnight ago that Jason Wilcox had bungled recruitment this summer, an assessment that seemed to be supported by Amad Diallo. Bruno Fernandes had a point in Como. Michael Carrick had picked the wrong tactics for the occasion. One of the most significant problems at Old Trafford is that the wrong executives, appointed by the wrong owners, are not exploiting the financial heft that United, even loaded with debt, still have. Another is that Carrick is not a good enough coach to paper over the cracks.

Those weren't the problems at Stamford Bridge on Saturday. This was a game lost for United by senior players. Fernandes and Amad, who is now 24 and has played over 100 games for the club, partly number among them. It is rarely wise to over-index on anyone missing chances; perhaps only Amad's last shot of the first half could reasonably have been termed one he should have scored. Then again, if you've got notes about tactics, you had best exploit the mismatches that come your way.

Whether through Chelsea's early disorganization or Carrick's adjustments -- which included center forward Bryan Mbeumo peeling off to the right and taking center backs with him -- Amad and Fernandes were afforded space and time to excel. Had they exploited them in the first half, United would have been firmly in the ascendancy.

Perhaps United heads would have melted anyway. It does not seem to take much to unleash a chain reaction of mental anguish on this team. One clumsy error begets two or three more, typified by Morgan Rogers' opener. Thirty percent individual brilliance, his clipped finish was as much a function of no one defending the space he was running into. Peter Bankes had the best view of proceedings as Andrey Santos went steaming in on fresh air.

"When you concede a goal it's never a good goal to concede. Morgan went through the middle of us. The game was in the balance, and to concede like that was," said Carrick, pausing as if catching himself before he said something he regretted. "Yeah it was a big moment for sure. I'm just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now."

From there the task fell to Martinez to escort Chelsea across the finishing line. An arm on the midriff was not enough to slow Rogers' advance, so the next time their paths crossed, the Argentine went altogether more physical, rugby-tackling the attacker as he was making his way away from goal. It wasn't just that it was a clear yellow-card tackle; Martinez didn't even stop the attack.

It took two more hacks from Martinez and Diogo Dalot before the ball ran away from Rogers. The resulting free kick was cleared for a corner, at which the man they call The Butcher thought it was wiser to start carving up Wesley Fofana than defend the delivery into the box.

Martinez was the most obvious culprit, but right across the field United flatlined the moment Chelsea scored their first. Even the 13 minutes between Rogers' goal and the contest effectively ending with a Cole Palmer penalty saw a string of players lose the run of themselves. Carlos Baleba had hardly excelled beforehand, but passes he was clipping with a pitching wedge before were now being smacked around with a driver. United could not pass their way out of the pressure that Chelsea applied to them in their own half. Free kicks flew to no one in particular, although perhaps it shouldn't have been surprising that no one was connecting with balls in the air when all their heads were on Mars.

What follows will be the usual psychodrama of Manchester United, all the more so if results go against them and they find themselves in the bottom three at the end of the weekend. At the time Carrick was asked about it, that was the position United occupied, with Nottingham Forest drawing at Brentford. "You've got to keep moving forward and winning games, it's as simple as that. There's no words that make it any different. You've got to move forward and win football matches, it's as simple as that."

It does not look simple. Their nine-game winless run is United's longest since 1988. With games against Roma and Aston Villa to come, double figures seems a real risk. Carrick confirmed he will be in charge for the first of those games on Tuesday night, but the two-week sacking window that is a November international break looms large. And yet, if the United hierarchy has backed its manager after he did bungle the tactics against Como, how could his sacking be justified when his players took events out of the coach's control?

Carrick certainly had the backing of the traveling fans, who went through the full repertoire of chants against the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Wilcox and the new stadium. All those grievances are well merited, but this was only a game lost by the executives in the sense that they should long ago have dispensed with some of the underperformers, with or without the offer of a transfer fee.

There will be the next round of the familiar debates on ownership and on how long Carrick might last. All of those will start from what these players did wrong. They are a constant through line in the perma-crisis, garlanded with individual awards, bedecked with honors for their international side and chronically incapable of delivering to the standards that they demand of others at United.

#1164. The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Karen Hinxman leads the White Rose University Consortium, a strategic partnership between the universities of York, Leeds and Sheffield, UK.

Research independence can create career uncertainty.Credit: molchanovdmitry/iStock via Getty

Early-career researchers are well aware of the uncertainties that an academic career can bring. Nevertheless, many expect that if they remain in academia, their careers will progress in a relatively familiar way: after completing a doctorate, they will move into a postdoctoral position, establish research independence, obtain a permanent post and, eventually, enter a more settled stage of academic life.

The conversations that my colleagues and I have had with established researchers while working on the White Rose Established Researchers project — a collaboration between the UK universities of Leeds, Sheffield and York that aims to support career development — suggest that career progression is often much less linear.

Research independence, which is characterized as a researcher’s ability to lead and sustain an original programme of research, is typically associated with the mid-career stage in academia. It brings with it a fresh set of challenges: how to sustain research while leading people, managing competing responsibilities and prioritizing the tasks that can have the greatest impact. The researchers whom we interviewed rarely spoke about having ‘made it’; instead, they described having to regularly refresh and revise how they think about their careers, in circumstances of increasing uncertainty.

It is striking how little attention has been paid to understanding the period between establishing research independence and the later stages of an academic career. Universities have invested heavily in supporting early-career researchers and have developed sophisticated programmes for senior leaders. Yet, relatively little attention has been given to the distinctive experiences of academics occupying the space between those career stages.

Our collaboration explored how established researchers experience the middle stage of their career. Across four months, we interviewed 27 established researchers, held two focus groups with them, sent them a follow-up survey to validate our findings and mapped institutional resources across the three universities.

Because no widely accepted definition of an established researcher exists, we defined them as “an academic who has achieved functional independence and institutional recognition in their research capacity, whilst continuing to develop their professional identity and navigate complex career transitions”.

The established-researcher career stage is characterized by a distinct research agenda, the capacity to secure and manage funding, a strong track record of scholarly outputs, recognition in relevant research communities and the ability to make substantive intellectual contributions to their field.

Across disciplines, established researchers described a shared experience of juggling various, often competing, responsibilities that span research, teaching, leadership, administration and collaboration. The challenge was rarely any individual role; instead, it was the continual negotiation of priorities across them.

As we analysed the interviews, we found that researchers were making sense of this complexity in different ways. To help to illuminate these recurring patterns, we outlined four personas that can be used to articulate different approaches to navigating the established stage of an academic career.

No researcher fits perfectly into a single persona. Many recognized aspects of themselves in more than one and described moving between them over time. But we developed these personas to understand how researchers think about success, make decisions and respond to the continuing complexity of academic life.

For some established researchers, academic life revolves around people as much as projects. Alongside developing their own research programmes, they recruit and train staff, secure funding and create opportunities for others. Many described an important transition from being the person who mainly conducts research to becoming the one who galvanizes the collective efforts of a team to enable research to happen.

Career planning strategies for scientists

Career planning strategies for scientists

For anyone hoping to lead a research group, this persona offers an important reminder: independence entails leadership, delegation, shaping research culture and balancing investment in others with maintenance of your own scientific expertise. Many researchers described the challenge of redefining success as their role shifted from doing research themselves to enabling the work of others. What got them to this point in their career was not always what was required to succeed in the next stage. This work is not routinely celebrated, yet it is fundamental to the long-term success of many research environments.

Many early-career researchers assume that becoming established means leading ever-larger groups. However, independent scholars organize their careers around sustained intellectual contribution: their influence comes from the ideas they develop and the scholarship they produce, pushing forwards thinking in their discipline. They might collaborate widely, but their work is characterized less by organizational expansion than by continuity of intellectual purpose.

One of their greatest challenges is protecting the quality thinking time that sustained scholarship requires while juggling the pressures of increasingly fragmented academic roles. Many also described the challenge of gaining recognition for forms of contribution that do not depend on large-scale grant funding, including editorial work, intellectual leadership and the development of scholarly communities that stimulate fresh debates and directions for research.

Some established researchers described careers centred on leading collaborative research on a large scale. Whether coordinating multidisciplinary teams, cross-institutional partnerships or large funded programmes, they bring together people, expertise and opportunities across several projects that do not necessarily form a single coherent research programme. Rather than building one permanent team, these researchers create successive collaborations that evolve as ideas, funding opportunities and partnerships emerge.

Their biggest challenge is maintaining a coherent sense of purpose while managing numerous projects, partnerships and opportunities simultaneously. As their portfolio grows, deciding which opportunities to pursue and which to decline becomes an increasingly important part of their professional development.

#1162. NWSL Decision Day storylines: Gotham, San Diego Wave chase Shield, last playoff spots up for grabs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There may still be a regular-season weekend left on the NWSL calendar, but for a few of the league's teams, Sunday's fixtures will see them slip into postseason mode a week in advance with plenty on the line on Decision Day.

The main characters will be Gotham FC and the Seattle Reign, each in control of their fate with different tasks ahead. Gotham have a chance to win the NWSL Shield for the very first time in Sunday's clash against the Utah Royals, with inconsistency in the final months of the season pushing the race for the trophy to the last day of the regular season. They are favored to collect the prize but have a formidable foe in the San Diego Wave, whose chances took a hit with last week's draw against the Boston Legacy.

The Reign, meanwhile, face the Orlando Pride in a game they must win to secure a spot in the playoffs. The North Carolina Courage are just two points behind them, and the Denver Summit three, with those two facing off against each other in the hope that the Reign slip up and hand one of them the chance to overtake.

Here's a look at what's to come as the NWSL regular season comes to a close.

Gotham have been favored to win the NWSL Shield for months, to the point that they had a seven-point lead in late summer. Even in a stretch of late-season ups and downs, though, their grip on first place has loosened but never slipped, leaving them well placed to win the trophy for the first time on Sunday. They boast a three-point lead over the Wave on Decision Day, a draw against the Royals enough to clinch the Shield, no matter what happens in the Wave's trip to Bay FC.

The bigger question for Gotham, though, is whether or not they will be at full strength a week before the playoffs begin. Jaedyn Shaw and Rose Lavelle both missed last week's 2-1 win at the Pride, while Shaw was also an unused substitute in a 1-0 loss at the Washington Spirit a week earlier. The pair have been Gotham's most impactful attackers this season, racking up a combined 22 goal contributions along the way; Shaw in particular has been both a goalscoring threat and a creative outlet, so much so that Gotham's attacking output fades considerably when she's not on the pitch. The league leaders might survive Sunday's clash without the U.S. women's national team standouts, the playoff-bound Royals set to enter the postseason with a middling defensive record.

Seven of the eight playoff spots are already booked, with three teams now vying for the final berth, and the margins will be tight for each of them. The Seattle Reign currently sit in eighth with 42 points, a win over the Pride enough to seal the deal. If they slip up, there are two teams in the waiting -- the North Carolina Courage and the Denver Summit, who play each other on Sunday. The Courage need to win and hope the Reign drop points to land in the top eight, while the Summit need to win plus a Reign loss to make the playoffs in their inaugural season.

There's a layer of unpredictability naturally baked into the scenario. The Reign not only have the easiest path -- win and they're in -- but they face a team whose playoff hopes were dashed some time ago. Their defense has really propped them up, conceding just 33 goals despite posting 39.96 expected goals against this season. Their rivals have their own strengths, the Summit finding form thanks to Lindsey Heaps' seven goals and three assists since her midseason arrival. The Courage, meanwhile, have this season's cheat code in Ashley Sanchez and speaking of...

With 20 goals this season, Sanchez's MVP argument writes itself at this point, but she has a chance to bolster her campaign on Sunday and make history along the way. She would set the NWSL's single-season goalscoring record if she scores against the Summit, while that goal or an assist would allow her to break Temwa Chawinga's single-season goal contributions record. It would be a worthy reward for Sanchez, whose conversion to left wing this season has been transformational and resulted in a well-earned return to the national team, thrusting her fully into the conversation for a spot on next summer's Women's World Cup roster. It is almost inconceivable, then, that her powers alone will not at least guarantee the Courage a spot in the postseason. Then again, they have maybe been overly reliant on Sanchez's form, the winger contributing to nearly half of the team's goals this campaign. They have been sunk, though, by a leaky defense, the Courage ranking in the league's bottom six for goals conceded. Missing the playoffs is unlikely to jeopardize Sanchez's MVP case, but it will speak to the Courage's limitations if they cannot sneak above the playoff line on the final day of the regular season.

Published: 17:16 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EDT, 2 November 2026

Jack Grealish was pictured enjoying a cracking night out in Newcastle last year. Here, his Everton team-mates had just as good a time, albeit in a far more sober state.

The Manchester City loanee was left at home after last week’s ‘breach of club discipline’. At least, home is where the club hoped he would be.

And, if he was, Grealish would have watched Everton record a deserved win. He might even have raised a toast, so accomplished an away performance was this.

David Moyes had dropped the winger for last Thursday’s 3-1 win over Newcastle in the Carabao Cup after he missed training following another alleged night on the town. And again, without him, they were too good for Matthias Jaissle’s sorry and directionless Newcastle.

It is the Toon Army, rather, in need of a bender right now. They really aren’t very good - no shots on target before injury-time - and it is remarkable to think they would have gone seventh with victory. That position is now occupied by Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish and won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break. The scoreline was not a reflection of their superiority.

Jaissle said: ‘We were not brave enough to break the line and play on the ground. We saw it in training, but there was almost nothing to see from these aspects in the game.

Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish, won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs, yet they were hiding en mass here

‘We have a clear identity of how we want to play - to bring the opposition in stressful situations high in the pitch. We spoke about creating one-on-one situations. The plan was not to play the long balls.’

The opening half hour had been a side-show in two managers betraying varying degrees of frustration. Jaissle buried his fist in his palm every time Everton played through his team at will. And Moyes muttered expletives when his side were unable to take advantage. It was clear he sensed this was there to be won. It was less clear how they would achieve that when Barry was swiping at fresh air six yards from goal.

Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 4; Dedic 4, Schar 5, Burn 5, Hall 5; Gonzalez 4 (Steur 64, 6), Joelinton 4 (Ramsey 76, 5); Elanga 4 (Murphy 76, 5) Willock 4 (Wissa 64, 5), Barnes 5; Osula 4.

Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; O’Brien 7, Tarkowski 7, Branthwaite 7, Mykolenko 7; Garner 7, Armstrong 7; Rohl 6, DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 6; Barry 7.

By the 28th minute, the home fans were booing after yet another aimless long ball. Vertical football, Jaissle has called it, getting the ball forward quickly. Yet more boos on the whistle for half-time told you the locals fear they are going backwards. Everton’s Harrison Armstrong, the half’s brightest midfielder, had only just swiped wide from 12 yards when he should have scored, and that would have been deserved.

The Toon Army were soon cheering, when a fella in jeans kicked a ball through a hole to win a trip to Las Vegas. It was the first effort on target by anyone on the field all evening. Newcastle’s first-half woe was summed up by one free-kick, worked short, that was then chipped straight out of play by Amar Dedic. Jaissle shot to his dugout to watch a replay of what had gone wrong - someone should have told him such footage could not be re-shown pre watershed.

The first effort on target brought the first goal in the 49th minute, and it was no surprise when it came Everton’s way. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall played the sort of pass of which Newcastle were seemingly incapable - low, incisive and accurate - and that set Tyrique George away. His shot was not particularly hard, but then Lukas Hornicek’s attempt to save it was not particularly convincing. As the ball squirmed through his grasp, Barry was quickest to follow up for a tap-in. Newcastle appealed offsides against both George and the scorer, but the truth was that Everton’s players were just sharper in every phase. The time afforded to the excellent Dewsbury-Hall to pick that pass was also a scandal.

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs. They were hiding en mass here. The head coach looked to his bench and called for the popular midfielder Sean Steur. The Dutch teenager’s popularity has been enhanced by him not being in the side of late. The cheer for his introduction, as replacement for the leaden-booted Nico Gonzalez, was almost as big as for the sharp-shooter in Levi’s.

Immediately, Steur impacted. From one smart pass to Harvey Barnes the winger crossed and Anthony Elanga almost stole in to score at the far post. The Geordies have been right to call for his involvement in a team so void of inspiration and positive energy.

It was not long, however, before a chorus of ‘attack, attack, attack’ emerged from the Gallowgate End, and that is never a good sign. Substitute Jacob Ramsey was then sent off for a second booking to compound the home misery.

Meanwhile, the fan bound for Vegas was probably checking for the next flight.

#1151. Where have all the saucers flown?

To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jeff Hecht is based in the Boston area where he writes factual articles about science and technology to make a living and science-fiction stories to stimulate the imagination, many of them for Nature Futures.

Holding her lunch box, Lili scanned the noon break area at the Exotic Destinations travel show. The middle-aged travel agents chattering among themselves ignored her, but a tall Black woman with snow-white hair waved.

Recognizing her from the session on tourism on the Extraterrestrial Highway, Lili walked over to ask, “May I join you?”

“Certainly,” the woman said. “My name’s Bettye, with an e at the end. I noticed you at the Extraterrestrial Highway session.”

“I’m Lili, with two l’s, two i’s and no y at all, and I saw you there. What did you think of their space alien experience?” She sat down to unpack her lunch.

“It’s changed tremendously since I was young,” Bettye said. “My parents just hoped to see a flying saucer on a long trip across the southwestern desert. Now they have cheesy roadside attractions with animated space aliens waving outside the door.”

Intrigued, Lili asked “What was it like back then?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

“Flying saucers were a mystery in the sixties; everybody wanted to see one. Papa was an Air Force mechanic, and pilots told him they had seen saucers. The Byrds sung about hitching a ride on a saucer. Papa always looked for saucers.”

“Do your stories help sell tours?” Lili asked.

“I wish I had travel stories, but my parents were too poor to take vacations after they immigrated from Hong Kong.”

Bettye grinned. “Oh, we loved telling those stories about looking for flying saucers, but we had to be careful we didn’t scare anyone.”

Bettye sipped her iced tea and sat back. “I saw my first saucer when we were driving through the desert. Papa drove at night because our old station wagon didn’t have air conditioning. The Moon was bright so we could see the foothills and the cacti. I fell asleep, but woke when Papa stopped. He and Mama whispered and pointed at a moonlit saucer parked a little ways away. A hatch opened and two aliens got out and walked towards us. Mama said we better go, but the car wouldn’t start. The aliens wore pale green suits and carried metal boxes that looked like old telephones. I waved, and they waved back.”

“A little,” Bettye said. “Then the boxes started talking English voices like we heard on the radio. Mama hushed me when I giggled.”

“They asked us to fly them over the mountains and tell them about the scenery. Papa laughed and said our car couldn’t fly. They said theirs could, and Mama got them to pay us to guide them. Mama was scared because she had never flown, but Papa and I had a great flight. After we landed, the aliens asked if we would guide other aliens on trips.”

“Oh yes. Papa took me along and we had a great time guiding the alien tours. They were very friendly and what they paid let me go to college.”

“That was a very successful business,” Lili said. “How long did it last?”

Bettye nodded. “Several years, until a saucer flew too close to an Air Force base. A pilot at the base jumped into a fighter and flew towards us. Papa told the aliens to fly away because the fighter might shoot us down, but their speaking boxes said ‘no civilized beings would do that’.”

“The fighter shot a missile at us. Then one alien pointed something at the missile and it vanished. The other alien pointed a box at the plane and made it move with what he called a force field. He made it land on the road. The pilot opened the door and ran away while we watched the alien melt the plane.”

#1149. Jürgen Klopp faces myriad of issues after rough start with Germany

Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't made an immediate impact, but he is not bowed.

Four games, three goals, two draws, one loss and one win. Jürgen Klopp would have hoped for better results from his first international break as Germany coach. But though the comfortable win over Serbia (2-0), draws against the Netherlands (1-1) and Greece (0-0) and a shock loss to Greece (0-1) in Germany leave them third out of four in their Nations League group, Klopp saw mostly positives.

"Everyone showed what they're made of; everyone earned their place. We've shown signs that we can do some things better than people gave us credit for. I wanted to get something going, and I definitely saw that happen," he said after Sunday's 0-0 draw in Thessaloniki.

For all the positivity of the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach, the four matches have, in reality, been a mixed bag for Germany.

Having fallen in the last 32 of the 2026 World Cup and exited in the group stage in 2022, Germany's footballing stock has never been lower.

Klopp tried to address this by casting his net wider, announcing a 44-man squad that split over the matches. He then said this would be a one off, but that his strategy of trying to find a diamond in the relative rough who could adapt to the international game had given him valuable insights.

"Hard work, lots of information — these guys are brimming with talent," he said of those given a surprise opportunity.

"People were saying that German soccer was at rock bottom and that there was no talent. ... They're not lacking in talent."

While Klopp may have seen potential, and has credit in the bank from his past work, he will need to turn that into results before too long.

While much has been said about Klopp's success in imprinting his trademark Gegenpressing (counter-press) style early on, he is also a coach who places a high value on connection. Throughout the international break, he has worn a cap emblazoned with the slogan "Einer von 83 millionen” (One of 83 million) in a reference to the German population and an attempt to unify in a country divided by the rise of the far-right AfD party.

He addressed the issue in his opening press conference and then reiterated his position after some social media users branded the team "not white enough" after their loss to Greece.

"There is no reason to give these people any thought. They aren't getting any of my attention. I have little time for stupidity in real life and none on social media either," Klopp said in answer to a question posed by DW.

As well as speaking honestly about his country, Klopp has been open with his new players.

"He has a very good rapport with every player. He tries to reach out to every player and make them feel good, that they're important and that they deserve to be here," said Florian Wirtz, who went on to label his coach as a "master" at managing relationships.

With limited time together, forming bonds between player, coach and country can elevate a national team. It may prove to be more important than any tactical plans.

One of the key men in the more senior squad that started the opener against the Netherlands, Kai Havertz limped off after 29 minutes. He was replaced by Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib while Nick Woltemade (on loan at Juventus from Newcastle) and Jonathan Burkhardt, also Frankfurt, were also tested up front over the four games.

None of the replacements scored, with Woltemade guilty of a particularly bad miss against Serbia and Burkhardt having a goal disallowed against Greece on Sunday. While all have potential and have enjoyed strong patches of form in their careers, none is tried and tested at the top level, and none is playing in the Champions League. With Havertz being somewhat injury prone, Klopp needs someone to emerge as a viable backup.

Injury is also, sadly, beginning to be a major feature of Jamal Musiala's career. He picked up a thigh injury in the warmup to the Netherlands game that may keep him out for a month. He's also missed games this season due to a neurological condition and missed the first half of last season with a broken leg, which came soon after another lengthy spell out. At his best, he is probably Germany's brightest attacking spark, but it's been a while since that level has been seen.

For Wirtz, the issue is slightly different. He was excellent in the win over a limited Serbia team, scoring one and creating the other. It was a reminder of a talent that has been largely dormant at Liverpool where he's shown his creative best only in glimpses. He followed it up with a decent display against Greece but saw Burkahrdt inadvertently block his goalbound header. There were signs Klopp's system may suit him.

"He's really gotten us on board with his philosophy," said Wirtz of his coach. "I enjoy it myself, too. I get to show my strengths when we have possession."

Klopp will need more of the same from Wirtz, who captained the side in Greece, if Germany are to move forward.

#1147. From Jose Mourinho's Sevilla disaster to Erik ten Hag's dismal group stage exit: Man United's litany of Champions League humiliations since Sir Alex Ferguson - as Michael Carrick fights for his job ahead of Roma clash

Published: 18:02 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 18:29 EDT, 2 November 2026

Michael Carrick and Manchester United are enduring the club's worst start to a league season in 40 years, with the Red Devils languishing in 17th place.

Their woes in recent years have been well documented, with the club seemingly incapable of finding anyone to match the glory days under Sir Alex Ferguson.

Since his departure in 2013, they have had eight managers – seven of whom have managed them in Europe's biggest competition.

The three-time champions of Europe have performed particularly poorly in the Champions League in that time, not making it past the quarter-finals once in seven attempts.

They have won less than half of their Champions League fixtures since Ferguson left – and only 34 per cent in the current decade.

Carrick brought United back into the Champions League last season but since being given the permanent role has hit shocking form

And they will be lucky to even reach that stage this season if they continue to play as they have been in the competition, losing to Atletico Madrid away and being embarrassed by Champions League debutants Como.

With United set to take on Roma on Tuesday in their fourth game of the competition, Daily Mail Sport takes a look at how each manager on United's carousel has fared in the Champions League... and where it unravelled for all of them.

It feels as if it has been an age since David Moyes took the reins at Old Trafford. The Scotsman had a torrid time in his ten-month spell at United.

His tenure was characterised by embarrassing losses, a lack of consistency and an inability to transition from the old regime.

Moyes was sacked in April after a 2-0 loss to his old Everton side that ended United's hopes of a top-four finish for that season. He was already under serious pressure having been dumped out of the Champions League in the quarter-finals by Bayern Munich.

Moyes was handpicked by Ferguson to replace him but didn't even last a season at United

The current Everton manager oversaw a 1-1 draw at home in the first leg, with Nemanja Matic's goal being cancelled out by Bastian Schweinsteiger – who moved to Old Trafford a year later. But Bayern – managed by Pep Guardiola – quickly responded to Patrice Evra's goal in the second leg to win it 3-1.

They had to battle to even get that far, with a comfortable group stage – four wins and two draws – being followed by an embarrassing 2-0 defeat at Olympiacos in the first leg of the last 16. A Robin van Persie hat-trick in the second leg spared their blushes.

The big Dutchman came to United with a stellar CV having won both the Champions League and UEFA Cup with Ajax in the 90s, as well as league titles in Spain and Germany.

And he seemed the exact kind of serial winner who would be the perfect replacement for Ferguson, but it just didn't work out. Van Gaal spent heavily in the market when he arrived - most notably breaking the British transfer record to secure the services of Angel Di Maria for £59.7million - but he simply couldn't find his feet in England.

Van Gaal had just the one season in the Champions League with United before leaving, and it was possibly the most disastrous since Ferguson's departure.

They were placed in a group with Wolfsburg, PSV and CSKA Moscow, and were dumped out at the earliest possible stage, finishing third in the group with just eight points. They fell into the Europa League and - after overturning a disastrous 2-1 defeat by Danish side Midtjylland in the first leg of their last-32 game - were sent packing by Liverpool.

Joining in 2016 after being sacked by Chelsea, Jose Mourinho immediately got busy in the market.

And initially it seemed as if he was going to make it work. Paul Pogba and Zlatan Ibrahimovic arrived and United won their first three games. Although their league form dipped, they did go on to win the League Cup and the Europa League in that first season.

But then it all began to fall away. Like Van Gaal and Moyes before him, Mourinho only got one try at his favourite competition with United, and exited in a less than graceful manner.

Jose won the Europa League whilst in Manchester but never really found success in the big competition

He may have won it with Porto in 2004 and Inter six years later but at United he only got as far as the round of 16, and crashed out after a 2-1 home defeat by Sevilla following a 0-0 draw in the first leg.

Recently Jose revealed that his relationship with the Red Devils was very nearly different. In his new Netflix biopic, Mourinho, he said that he had agreed to take over straight after Ferguson - only to be lured back to Chelsea by Roman Abramovich instead. Who knows how he would have fared at Old Trafford if he had joined three years earlier.

Mourinho's successor also had an excellent start to life in the United dugout but ended up being hounded out after a tumultuous three years.

When Ole was at the wheel, at first it seemed like United were on course to return to the big time however, slowly but surely, it became clear that it wasn't going to work out.

Solskjaer is one of two men on this list to have won the Champions League with United as a player and the Norwegian scored arguably the most historic goal in United's European history, getting the dramatic winner in the 1999 final.

And he is probably the only gaffer since Ferguson to have had a positive memorable moment in the competition. It came in Paris in March of 2019, shortly after he took over. After losing 2-0 at home in the first leg of the tie they looked like they were already out but miraculously Ole masterminded a 3-1 victory and won on away goals.

Unfortunately that is where the good times as a manager in the Champions League end. After the PSG win United were beaten 4-0 on aggregate by Barcelona and then didn't make it into the competition for the 2019-20 season.

They did return with Ole in 2020-21 - only to be knocked out in the group stage, finishing third in a group with PSG, RB Leipzig and Turkish side Basaksehir. They went on to reach the Europa League final that year - losing to Villarreal on penalties - and Solskjaer was gone in November, before the end of next season's group stage.

Taking over as interim manager until the end of the 2021-22 campaign - following a caretaker spell from a certain Michael Carrick - Austrian Rangnick was in charge for just three European games.

The final game of the group stage saw a 1-1 draw with Swiss side Young Boys, with Mason Greenwood scoring United's goal.

Then they took on Atletico Madrid in the last-16, and after a 1-1 draw away, were sent packing with a 1-0 second-leg defeat at Old Trafford.

Renan Lodi's header for Atletico Madrid sent United crashing out under Ralf Rangnick

Rangnick's spell at United is best remembered for his forthright assessments of the club's dire situation, and he famously likened their situation to that of a patient needing open-heart surgery.

'You don’t even need glasses to see and analyse where the problems are,' he said. 'Now it’s about how do we solve them? It’s not enough to do some minor amendments. In medicine you would say that this is an operation of the open heart.

'If this happens and everyone has realised that this has to happen and if people want to work together then it makes sense and I believe it doesn’t take two or three years to change those things. This can happen within one year.'

More than four years on, the fans are still waiting.

Erik ten Hag came in nine years after Ferguson's exit, and while he brought a League Cup and an FA Cup to Old Trafford it was not enough to stop him being sacked.

Like Van Gaal and Solskjaer, Ten Hag's United failed to make it past the group stage of the Champions League. He actually fared even worse than his predecessors by finishing rock bottom of the group in the 2023-24 season, after particularly rough losses away to Copenhagen and Galatasaray.

Like Van Gaal and Solskjaer, Ten Hag's United failed to make it past the group stage of the Champions League

After a dismal eighth-placed finish in the Premier League the FA Cup win over Manchester City ended that season on a high - and saved Ten Hag's job.

He even signed a contract extension that summer, but was ditched by October with United 14th.

Ruben Amorim, who replaced Ten Hag, did not manage United in the Champions League - though he did reach the Europa League final with them in 2025.

His sacking in January this year paved the way for Michael Carrick to join as interim and, in steering them to third place, ensured United were back at Europe's top table after two seasons away.

That also won him the permanent role, but Carrick has had a torrid start to the new campaign - winning just two of his side's 13 games in all competitions and setting a new club record for the longest winless streak in the Premier League era (nine).

One of those wins was in the Champions League against Azerbaijani minnows Sabah, but they followed that with the defeats by Atletico Madrid and Como.

Carrick will hope United can finally arrest this run of form at home to Roma on Tuesday, but it will not be easy with the Italians enjoying an excellent start to the season and currently sitting third in Serie A.

A win, however, could keep Carrick in a job and breathe some life into a United team that desperately needs it.

#1141. Euro plummets against US dollar: Has the next financial crisis begun?

The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal crisis at hand?

The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns about eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices.

The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down about 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 (€0.99) on Monday, the lowest level since early 2025.

Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist at Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields.

However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk."

The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly.

France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion).

France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office.

For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt.

The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely watched measure of EU financial stability.

The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic.

Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand.

"The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said.

Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added.

He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now.

Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability.

Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the leading candidate.

Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy.

Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament.

Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation.

"Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said.

A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods, particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports.

With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone.

Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believe such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

However, Amaro says the fact that further interest rate hikes are expected from the ECB this year, combined with the worsening inflation outlook, makes this a situation which needs to be managed and monitored very carefully.

"Euro weakness shouldn't be interpreted as an isolated development," he says. "If triggered by growing concerns about France's fiscal outlook, then the ECB would certainly want to thread that carefully given risks for the eurozone."

#1136. Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade

Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz have written to Ursula von der Leyen, calling for tougher EU mechanisms against unfair trade practices by other states. They name no names but seem to have China or the US in mind.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron sent a joint appeal to the European Commission on Monday, calling for tougher EU measures against unfair trade practices by other states.

They said that the existing instruments at the EU's disposal were no longer sufficient.

The appeal did not name any specific country but it seemed most clearly tied to Chinese trade policy, the EU's vast deficit with China, and its dependence on certain key raw materials. The other apparent candidate would be the US, not least under the current unpredictable trade policy stewardship of tariff-loving President Donald Trump.

It also came just a few days before the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, is set to visit Beijing.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for two new measures to be introduced in Brussels.

One would aim at ensuring diversification and preventing companies from becoming too dependent on suppliers from individual companies.

The other would allow another country to be excluded from access to the European single market on an expedited basis if exceptional circumstances made this necessary.

Merz and Macron wrote that this could be used in cases "where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions through political or economic means, leading to serious and systematic distortions of our single market."

The French and German leaders, both struggling to balance economic growth and public spending, said the EU's struggles to maintain global competitiveness and its dependencies on certain suppliers of core materials led to "geoeconomic risks."

"The open and rules-based trading system is being massively compromised by the instrumentalization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances," they wrote. "All this undermines the level competitive playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign core industrial producer and our capacity for innovations, which leads to increasing dependencies and geoeconomic risks."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Monday's letter is what's known in EU diplomatic circles as a "non-paper." These are nonbinding, informal documents shared between EU member states and institutions that are supposed to propose ideas and initiate discussions without officially committing to a position.

It recommends authorizing the Commission to exclude a country from single market access in extreme situations if it sees the need — currently a complicated process that would take some time to arrange and requires approval from member states.

It suggests reversing this process: allowing the Commission to take the step independently, but with member states then having the chance to block it with a qualified majority vote, which the EU currently defines as a vote by a minimum of 55% of member states that also represents a minimum of 65% of the bloc's total population.

The EU's trade deficit with China is vast and growing. The EU put the figure at around €360 billion (roughly $400 billion) in 2025, though China's statisticians reached a more modest tally of $292 billion.

The bloc is also particularly dependent on China for a number of raw materials, not least rare earths, and is increasingly reliant on both the US and China for high-tech imports and services, particularly in computing and the so-called AI sector.

The EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, visits China this week for talks, ahead of an EU leaders' summit next week, on October 15-16. Sefcovic said earlier this year that he hoped to see "tangible results by October" on the question of trade with China, although whether these will materialize is an open question.

Beijing has warned that it could retaliate with changes of its own after learning of the EU's plans, if it perceives a need to.

#1133. AI models keep hacking real systems during tests. What does this mean?

AI models have repeatedly broken into real commercial and government systems during safety tests during 2026. Cybersecurity researcher Thorsten Holz explains what that means, and why he isn't expecting a robot uprising.

Let's start with people's real world fears about AI. Here's a sample of people we asked:

Sebastian, 22, says it'll be an AI-powered robot uprising that finally wipes out humanity: "I think that'll take some time," he says, admitting his dystopia owes a lot to the 2004 film "I, Robot."

Luisa, 19, has heard the rumors too. Her fear is what happens when these tools get into the wrong hands. "I'm more afraid of people," she says. "Powerful people."

Pilar, 25, is pessimistic about humanity's prospects. "The world is going down," she says. "Hopefully after my lifetime."

In 2026, AI systems have repeatedly slipped out of human control — and at some of the world's largest AI companies.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta have all disclosed in 2026 that their AI agents escaped the controlled test environments.

Agents are AI systems that don't just answer questions but act — running code, browsing the web, clicking through systems — on their own.

"It feels a bit crazy how powerful these models have become." Holz told DW. "I didn't anticipate they'd be so obsessed with solving tasks and that they'd start to do things we never [foresaw]."

Holz is one of 16 authors of ExploitGym. ExploitGym is an AI benchmark published in May 2026 by a team led by the University of California, Berkeley, with researchers from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. It is a standardized test of cybersecurity capabilities and vulnerabilities.

Its 898 challenges test whether AI agents can turn known software bugs into working attacks. Each one runs inside a sandbox — a sealed-off digital space, cut off from the internet, so nothing the agent does can reach anything real. That's the theory, anyway.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI models had escaped from their sandbox.

They were running an internal ExploitGym test with the models' safety refusals switched off, a setting that lets evaluators measure what a model is capable of rather than what it will decline to do.

Failing the task, the models went looking for a shortcut instead, and found a flaw in the software meant to keep them sealed in. It let them onto the open internet.

From there they worked out that Hugging Face, a site where AI developers store and share models and data, probably held the answer to the test.

So, they broke in and went looking for it, organizing the effort on message boards they set up themselves. The behavior was not instructed, according to OpenAI's account of the incident.

Hugging Face detected the intrusion and shut it down before OpenAI connected it to its own test. No customer data was reportedly taken.

"What happened is really a bit of science fiction," Holz said.

Then, Google confirmed that its Gemini model had guessed or found login credentials and accessed three real companies' websites during a May test run by the independent evaluator Irregular — an intrusion Google learned of in July 2026 and disclosed weeks later.

Anthropic's and Meta's escapes happened in sandboxes run by the same firm, which has said it notified the labs in late July 2026 and that it has since fixed the flaws.

In late September 2026, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had broken into a statistics portal belonging to Medicare, Australia's public health system, reaching non-public files and writing data into a government server. No patient records were reportedly touched.

The incidents have revived older fears. If agents can program each other, where does that end? Could it lead to what philosopher Nick Bostrom has called a "paperclip maximizer"?

Bostrom's thought experiment imagines a machine given one simple goal: Make as many paperclips as possible.

The machine pursues the task so single-mindedly that it eventually treats humans as raw material standing in the way.

"For the intermediate future, I do not see any kind of scientific evidence that there could be this super intelligence that autonomously decides, 'Okay, let's kill,'" said Holz.

Rogue software needs vast datacenters to run, he said, which makes it visible. And the internet is built from parts that can keep working independently of one another.

But the AI escapes and hacks in 2026 were noticed late. Google learned of Gemini's intrusions two months after they happened, and OpenAI told Australia about the Medicare breach nearly three months after the event.

Holz said he expects a different kind of threat: Bad actors turning capable AI on critical infrastructure, mass compromise of ordinary machines, or chatbots used to manipulate information at scale and destabilize politics.

No, Europe cannot easily compete with China, according to experts.

France's Mistral and Germany's open-source Soofi project lag behind the frontier labs — a handful of US and Chinese firms building the most advanced models. Europe lacks the datacenter capacity to train systems at that scale, which leaves it dependent on non-European models, and largely subject to US or Chinese export controls.

For Holz, the more pressing gap is expertise. "What we definitely need to see is how we can build up more competence in the area of security, AI, and especially the intersection of both," he said.

Be skeptical of what the companies themselves claim, Holz said. They have a financial interest in the conversation, he said, particularly ahead of a stock market listing. "There's also fear mongering, or a bit of hype, about how advanced these models get."

Holz uses AI daily, as do his children. His nine-year-old generates coloring book pages. His 12-year-old uses it for homework, but has already learned the hard way that it lies and that "it's sometimes wrong."

#1129. Nobel Prize in literature: How the winner is secretly chosen

Can Xue is considered one of this year's favorites; Margaret Atwood and Salman Rushdie are other strong contenders. But what goes on behind the scenes in the selection of the Nobel Prize in literature?

On Thursday, October 8, at around 1:00 p.m. CEST, all eyes in the literary world will be set on Stockholm.

That's when the new permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, will hold a press conference to announce the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature, marking the end of a lengthy selection process that officially began a year earlier.

The Swedish Academy is the body responsible for awarding the prize. Its 18 members consist of writers, professors and intellectuals.

In September of the previous year, the Academy's Nobel Committee sends forms to hundreds of individuals and organizations eligible to submit nominations for the Nobel Prize in literature.

According to the Nobel Prize website, these include professors of literature and linguistics at universities and colleges, previous Nobel laureates in literature and the heads of writers' associations that represent the literary community in their respective countries. Anyone from one of these groups who has not received a form may also submit a nomination.

"The list can reach 200 names per year of nominated authors," explains Gisele Sapiro, research director at France's National Centre for Scientific Research. She studies how the Nobel Prize, as a global institution, influences the international circulation of literature, power dynamics in the literary world and translation markets.

"The committee can also add names itself, such as authors who were nominated in previous years," she says.

In the spring, the Nobel Committee then selects five names through a multistage process and presents them to the Academy. Over the summer, Academy members read the nominees' works and discuss them. The Academy always announces the decision in early October.

As for the criteria the Academy uses to make its decision, it prefers to keep them to itself.

The public doesn't learn which nominees missed out until 50 years later — that's how long the Academy waits before releasing the list.

Sometimes decades pass between an author's first nomination and actually receiving the prize. Danish writer Johannes V. Jensen, who won the Nobel Prize in literature in 1944, waited 40 years. Doris Lessing received the award in 2007 after 35 years, while Thomas Mann, who won in 1929, had to wait 27 years.

In his will, Alfred Nobel, the prize's founder, stipulated that it should be awarded to the person who had produced "the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction." That leaves plenty of room for interpretation.

According to Gisele Sapiro, the Academy aims to honor ambitious, influential literature that has, for example, given rise to a new literary movement. "At the same time, the work has to be universal, being able to transcend its own culture," she says.

Translations can be one indication of this. "I noted in my research, however, that all the laureates since 1990 had been translated into English, French and German — except for Abdulrazak Gurnah [the Tanzanian-British 2021 Nobel laureate], who had not been translated into German before winning — meaning that I think these three languages are the most important," Sapiro explains.

Sapiro says it is also a major advantage if nominees have already won other major literary awards, such as the International Man Booker Prize, the Cervantes Prize or the Büchner Prize.

Politics can also influence the Swedish Academy's decisions.

On several occasions, the prize has gone to writers who openly opposed the regimes in their home countries, such as Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich in 2015. She is an outspoken critic of authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko.

Genre, on the other hand, does not matter. In the past, laureates have been honored not only for novels but also for poetry and plays. In 2016, singer-songwriter Bob Dylan received the prize for his song lyrics.

So far, only 33 of the 122 laureates have come from outside Europe. There is also a clear gender imbalance: only in the past eight years have men and women alternated as winners, significantly increasing women's share of the total number of laureates to 14.9%.

#1123. Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant

Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival efforts from Netflix.

Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.

The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.

The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.

The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.

The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.

"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.

Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.

The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.

Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

#1121. How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

Science in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: 22% of participants in that nation said they had ‘no trust at all’ in science in 2025. Credit: Thomas Imo/Photothek via Getty

Trust in science and researchers has fallen following the COVID-19 pandemic, the largest survey of public confidence in science shows. Led by the global biomedical funder Wellcome in London and published on 10 October, it explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence (see ‘Trust in decline’).

“We should be paying attention to, and thinking about, what needs to be done to earn that trust,” says Philippa Michael, head of public initiatives at Wellcome, who led the project. This is the third survey of its kind conducted by Wellcome, following editions in 2018 and 2020.

The analysis points to a “mixed” picture that varies between countries and regions, says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia (see ‘Regional differences’).

The study also shows a connection between science and people’s broader experiences, including their perceived financial security, says Michael (see ’Money matters‘).

“If people feel economically insecure, then they’re going to feel a greater distance between themselves and science and scientists,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat, at Harvard Kennedy School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This disconnect “is not about science’s efficacy or its ability to fix problems”, he adds.

The survey found that countries where people reported high confidence in hospitals and health-care clinics were “more likely to have greater trust in science”, notes Michael. Levels of trust were also high in respondents who were confident in accessing health-care services when needed. “It’s really essential that science is credible, relevant and beneficial to people in their lives,” Michael adds.
